entries.title: Justice Department Appeals Judge’s Ban on Tree-Cutting at East Potomac Golf Course
entries.summary: President Donald Trump said his administration would appeal the “unconstitutional” decision by the federal judge.
entries.content:
The Justice Department is appealing a federal judge’s order blocking further tree removal at D.C.’s East Potomac Golf Course, escalating the fight over President Donald Trump’s planned overhaul of the historic public course.

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued the injunction Monday in a scathing opinion finding that challengers — a preservation group and golfers — were likely to prove the administration violated federal environmental law. Her order also requires 10 business days’ notice before other irreversible changes to East Potomac Park.

The government is now seeking to have that ruling overturned by a panel of judges in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia. The two-page notice does not explain the administration’s arguments for overturning the ruling.

Trump blasted Reyes late Monday, and announced that he’d appeal the judge’s “unconstitutional” decision.

“The judge has absolutely no right to hold up this very important and beautiful Project,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “We are asking the D.C. Circuit Court for immediate remedy.”

entries.title: Streamer Hasan Piker Hits Scott Jennings With a $72 Million Defamation Suit
entries.summary: Piker alleges Jennings aired a fabricated video of him calling for “Black voters to be lynched.”
entries.content:
Leftist livestreamer Hasan Piker sued commentator Scott Jennings in federal court Tuesday, seeking more than $72 million in damages over allegations that Jennings falsely depicted him as advocating the lynching of Black Americans.

Filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, the lawsuit brings claims of defamation, defamation by implication and false light. Piker addressed the suit on his Twitch stream Tuesday, saying “Guess the fucking cat’s out of the bag, huh?”

"This is not just about Scott Jennings, although he certainly messed up,” Piker continued. “This is about truth in the media. I think for far too long we have allowed Republicans to get away with saying whatever they want.”

The complaint alleges Jennings, who is also a CNN contributor, aired a manipulated video of Piker and attributed fabricated statements to him during an August episode of “The Scott Jennings Show.” It also accuses Jennings of using the altered footage to attack Democrats.

Jennings played the edited footage on his podcast during a segment criticizing Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s ties to Piker. He falsely portrayed Piker as advocating lynchings and suggested Black voters should consider supporting Republicans.

“Now El-Sayed’s best friend is out there calling for Black voters to be lynched,” Jennings said.

Jennings did not respond to a request for comment Tuesday night.

Piker has played the role of campaigner and fundraiser this midterm cycle, primarily focused on mobilizing younger voters — and particularly young men — toward campaigns like El-Sayed’s and progressive tickets.

His growing presence on the far left has drawn immense ire from Republicans and some establishment Democrats, who have sought to impede the momentum of the democratic socialist agenda by unearthing statements Piker has made on his daily livestreams, notably referencing his 2019 comments that “America deserved 9/11.”

While Piker has since apologized for those statements and argued over their context, his rhetoric has nonetheless become a common line of questioning for candidates he supports.

El-Sayed has routinely drawn condemnation for his decision to appear on Piker’s stream ahead of his Michigan primary victory.

In response to weeks of media scrutiny, Piker told Semafor in August he was considering bringing defamation lawsuits against Democratic and Republican critics.

He reiterated those statements during his Monday livestream. Piker said the lawsuit against Jennings has already become a “very costly endeavor” and told his viewers he planned to launch a fundraiser to bankroll that suit and possibly lawsuits against others in the future.

“I don't think you should be able to get away with lying like this, and if I don't put a stop to it, they're going to continue maliciously defaming others as they have done so this entire time,” he said.

entries.title: Ex-Biden Officials Want 2028 Democrats to Reject Biden and Trump Policies on Israel
entries.summary: They’re asking potential presidential candidates to pledge to reject controversial Israel-Gaza policies and to avoid hiring staff who shaped those policies.
entries.content:
As the 2026 midterm cycle concludes, eyes will soon turn to 2028 — and the crowded presidential field. And much like in this year’s races, the relationship between America and Israel is expected to play a central role. One group of former U.S. officials is getting a head start on working to shape candidates’ policies regarding America’s longstanding and increasingly controversial ally.

As polling shows that Americans’ favorability of Israel has hit historic lows, a dozen officials who resigned from the Biden administration over concerns about America’s role in the Israeli military campaign in Gaza released a pledge Wednesday for potential presidential candidates to sign. The pledge says signatories reject the Israel policies of Presidents Donald Trump and Joe Biden and promise to not hire former staffers who the group says fueled military destruction in Gaza and a humanitarian crisis among Palestinians.

“Senior Biden Administration officials who were architects of the Gaza policy are now actively white-washing their own roles in enabling genocide,” reads the pledge document, which was shared exclusively with The Washington Sun. “When faced with the opportunity to stand up in defense of our laws, they not only stayed silent, but worked resolutely in pursuit of illegal and wrongful ends in violation of both U.S. and international law. And they did so despite ample evidence and thorough internal warnings of the consequences.”

“We must ensure these officials can never again wield power in the name of the American people … not only as a consequence for their actions, but also as a deterrent,” the pledge document continues.

The pledge from the Biden-era resignees does not name specific officials. But Biden staffers, including Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk and deputy national security adviser Jon Finer, have argued they did not receive firm conclusions that their Gaza policy broke international law or American laws governing military support to partner countries. As secretary of state, Antony Blinken did receive recommendations from several State Department offices to penalize Israeli military units, but he did not take that step. Finer, McGurk and a representative for Blinken did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The new commitment has three components. First: enforcing U.S. law and pursuing American interests “without fear or favor” — a nod to concerns in the Biden era about political backlash for challenging Israel, and to complaints that Trump’s cooperation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu constitutes an “Israel-first” policy.

Second is a promise to “acknowledge the complicity of the United States government in Israel’s genocide in Gaza.” Roughly half of Democrats believe Israel has committed genocide, according to polling by The Associated Press.

The final part of the pledge is to avoid hiring any “past or present political appointee” who the group describes as “an architect, leader, defender, or key enabler” of unchecked U.S. backing for Israel.

Israel denies that it has committed a genocide and says it investigates claims of human rights violations. The International Criminal Court has issued warrants for Netanyahu and his former defense minister for war crimes and crimes against humanity. U.S. government lawyers repeatedly suggested Biden’s Gaza policy could violate international law.

Josh Paul, the first Biden-era resignee over Gaza, told The Sun that the group has discussed its pledge with several potential 2028 candidates. “I would not anticipate people signing on until they announce [their candidacies],” said Paul, who had served in the State Department for more than 11 years.

Several likely 2028 Democratic candidates have made opposition to U.S. policy in Gaza, including criticism of Biden’s approach, central to their political brands. They include Rep. Ro Khanna (California), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (New York) and Sen. Chris Van Hollen (Maryland). 

Spokespeople for Khanna and Ocasio-Cortez did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Van Hollen’s representative referred The Sun to comments the senator made in a recent interview.

Asked about officials like Blinken, McGurk and former National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan serving in a future Democratic administration during an interview with Zeteo this month, Van Hollen said: "People can change, but they have to be able to demonstrate that they fully understand exactly what went wrong and their role. ... I have not seen the kind of introspection and change that I think would be required.”

A spokesperson for Sullivan did not respond to a request for comment.

Paul suggested Republican candidates would also be welcome to sign, as doubts about Israel have grown among conservatives alongside mounting frustrations about Trump’s Iran war.

The backers of the pledge include former career diplomatic personnel, military officers, humanitarian experts and Biden political appointees.

“We want candidates to be aware that the officials who enabled Israel’s genocide in Gaza are politically toxic. If they try to hire them, they will face consequences from voters,” said Annelle Sheline, a former State Department official who was an organizer of the pledge.

It’s unclear whether such calls will succeed. Some of the possible Democratic presidential candidates are wary of using the term “genocide” to describe Israel’s actions. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the party’s 2024 nominee and the front-runner in most 2028 polling, has said the Biden administration should have used American leverage over Israel more forcefully but has largely avoided specific critiques of her former colleagues. And other groups that have typically influenced Democratic Party policy, planning and staffing have welcomed some of Biden’s top Gaza advisers to their ranks, including Blinken on the board of the Center for American Progress think tank, and Sullivan as a player in the organizations Foreign Policy for America and National Security Action.

The group that could ultimately hold the most sway in 2028 Democratic policies is the party’s financial backers.

“From a donor viewpoint, it's going to be hard for any candidate not to acknowledge the egregious behavior of the Biden administration,” Liam Connell, a longtime Democratic donor in the Chicago suburbs, told The Sun. “Some of the very centrist or right candidates may keep quiet about it, but nobody is going to defend it.”

Connell, who helped organize a donor letter to Biden’s team in 2024 saying the Gaza policy risked helping Trump, said he has seen a shift away from previous “reluctance” among donors to discuss America’s entanglement in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. He argued that the pledge is “pushing an open door.”

But another source involved in Democratic campaigns and fundraising suggested it would be complicated for the party to find unanimity on barring those involved in past Gaza policy from future service.

‘For every donor that finds them problematic, you'll find another donor that does not,” said the source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss private organizing efforts.

The source tied the chances of a reckoning over Gaza to an electoral calculation — specifically, the upcoming Senate race in Michigan, a crucial swing state where the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, is a prominent proponent of overhauling the U.S.-Israel relationship.

2028 campaigns, the source said, are “waiting to see if Abdul wins” to decide how much Biden’s Gaza record matters.

entries.title: The Capitals Aren’t Fans of This Weird Schedule, Either
entries.summary: Washington has played just twice in the last 10 days — the only stretch the team will have like this all season.
entries.content:
If you have not been enamored with this oddly quiet stretch of the Capitals’ schedule — neither have they.

“A little weird, for sure,” Washington defenseman Cole Hutson said.

“Kind of feels almost like college again, where you’re just practicing a lot,” said forward Ryan Leonard.

“I haven’t liked it all, to be honest with you,” Capitals head coach Spencer Carbery said.

The Capitals have played just twice in the last 10 days and have spent the entire time at home. No other portion of the schedule is like this for them — Washington will not have any other stretches this year with three days off before a single game followed by three days off after.

They are grateful for that.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“We’ve had some really productive video sessions,” Carbery said. “But these guys are in game mode. The practices are the practices.”

They return with a back-to-back: Washington faces the Flyers at home on Wednesday before facing the Predators on the road on Thursday.

A (very) informal survey of the locker room determined that the ideal schedule cadence is playing every other day. Some older players appreciate two days between games for extra recovery. But no one is an especially big fan of three days, as they have now experienced not once, but twice in the last week.

“It’s a little bit harder to get into a rhythm,” said forward Jordan Kyrou. “I would say the most ideal is playing three, maybe four times a week.”

(While offering his thoughts on a dream schedule, Kyrou made a pitch for some more afternoon puck drops, too: “I love 1 o’clock games,” he said. “Wake up, eat some breakfast, then you play.”)

Still, the recent schedule has offered some upsides. The extra practice sessions have meant extra time practicing the power play: Washington shuffled its units last week and is hoping to build on some modest recent momentum there. It has also offered some necessary recovery time for goalie Logan Thompson, who is currently on injured reserve, dealing with a lower body issue. He’s been able to practice each of the last two days. Carbery did not commit to a timeline for his return, but the practice showings have been a “good sign,” he said. And the extra downtime has given the newest member of the roster a chance to get acclimated.

The Capitals claimed defenseman Jack St. Ivany off waivers to fill the spot left open by Vincent Desharnais. Arguably the most promising blueliner for this roster so far, Desharnais had an emergency appendectomy last week, a procedure that will reportedly sideline him for at least a month. He’s not an easy presence to replace. (Literally: At 6’7”, Desharnais is the Capitals’ most imposing player.) He led the roster in plus-minus and proved critical early on in shoring up the defense, and his physicality will be sorely missed.

St. Ivany has appeared in 57 games over the last four seasons with the Penguins and Jets.

“He's shown that he can play in the league,” Carbery said of the 27-year-old. “It's now about solidifying himself and getting an opportunity and chipping away at one, two, 10, 20, 30, 40 games and showing that you can provide good, solid NHL minutes.”

St. Ivany said that he is excited for the chance to get out there and show what he can do. And following these long days off, so are most of his new teammates.

entries.title: Delegate on Deadline
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Oct. 28, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Robert White’s eligibility issues, the battle over foie gras and a Mystic abroad. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 8/10. We’ve been spoiled by a string of nearly perfect days. Today is still quite nice, just more clouds in the mix. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

Can he delegate? D.C. Council member Robert White, the Democratic nominee to be the District’s nonvoting congressional delegate, is racing against the clock.

A 1970 D.C. law mandates that a delegate cannot hold any other paid public office at the time of their election. The obscure provision puts White’s eligibility into question just days before voters decide on a race that was all but set to be a shoo-in, The Washington Sun’s Michael Brice-Saddler reports.

White told The Sun that his team is working “through a few options” to resolve the issue, while pushing back on claims that his campaign was caught off guard.

“This isn’t new to me,” White said. “We’ve had a legal theory on this for quite some time.”

What changed? The D.C. attorney general recently gave White a reading on the matter that he did not agree with or expect.

Now, he must either resign from the council before Tuesday and forfeit his final months in the role — which includes serving as housing committee chair at a fraught moment — or persuade his colleagues to consider changing the law by then with an emergency action. His team is waiting on additional clarity before sharing a final plan.

What is clear: “I’m not going to jeopardize going into Congress,” he told The Sun.





DUCK DIVE


The battle for foie gras is might come to DC voters. (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)This is a question D.C. residents won’t be able to duck: Should the city ban the sale of foie gras?

It’s not a hypothetical, but rather the heart of Initiative 86, which seeks to ban the production and sale of foods that result from the force-feeding of fowl — largely foie gras, the French delicacy that comes from the fattened livers of ducks and geese.

Residents and restaurateurs alike are divided on whether foie gras should be banned, The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports. Celebrity chef and humanitarian José Andrés is opposed; he thinks the city and world have bigger fish to fry.

“I don’t really like foie gras, but I do think restaurants should have the right to serve it,” Geoff Tracy of Chef Geoff’s told Martin.

But some voters do see how foie gras is made — essentially by force-feeding ducks and geese until their livers expand — as a problem. “I voted for it because it seems inhumane to me and unfair to the ducks,” said David Abramson, a Ward 1 voter who cast his ballot on Monday in Columbia Heights.

There is also a broader political question that some are asking: Have D.C.’s ballot initiatives gone too far? “I have an issue with national issues being dumped on D.C. residents, and I think this may be one such issue,” said Mayor Muriel Bowser, referring to the fact that a Colorado-based animal rights group has funneled hundreds of thousands of dollars into getting the initiative on the November ballot.

It’s now up to you, D.C. voters.





FROM THE DISTRICT

A federal judge has extended a ban on removing trees from East Potomac Golf Links, issuing a scathing 70-page opinion late Monday against President Donald Trump’s overhaul of the historic public course — with some more references to “The Lorax,” The Sun’s Gavin J. Quinton reports.

A few hours after the opinion was published, Trump took to Truth Social to air his grievances with U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes’ decision and reiterate his claim that the golf course will close Nov. 15 for its redevelopment. On Tuesday, Reyes ordered the Trump administration’s lawyers to respond to Trump’s post, which contradicts comments that Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward made in a hearing earlier this month that there were no plans to close the course that day. The government has until 3 p.m. today to submit its response.

Shady stuff: A digital 3D model created by The Washington Post shows that Trump’s proposed 250-foot triumphal arch would cast a shadow over presidential memorials, war monuments and thousands of graves in Arlington National Cemetery, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.

Police say a suspect in the killings of two children rapped about their shooting and was part of a group chat that celebrated the deaths, City Cast D.C. reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

Instead of data centers, Amazon will build more than 1,500 units of housing on George Washington University’s Ashburn campus, The Washington Business Journal reports. The tech company, which purchased the campus for $427 million earlier this year, axed the data center plan last week.

A sweet deal: An orthodontist in Reston is buying kids’ extra Halloween candy for a good cause, WTOP reports. Tisseront Orthodontics will give kids $1 for every pound of candy they bring in and match that figure in a donation to Children’s National Hospital. Tisseront’s staff then sends the candy to U.S. troops overseas.





FROM MARYLAND

Prince George’s County will officially be home to the nation’s second Sphere after county council members gave unanimous final approval on Tuesday to the plan for a $1.4 billion entertainment venue, Kendall reports.





PLAN YOUR WEEKEND

thewharfdiadelosmuertos11-01-25-1147.jpg (2000x1334, AR: 1.50)
For the seasonal: Dupont Circle Fall Festival, Pumpkin Patch and Bluegrass Jamboree, Saturday.

For ’80s enthusiasts: Eighties Mayhem Halloween Dance Party at the Black Cat, Saturday.

For the dead: Día de los Muertos celebration at The Wharf, Sunday.

For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here.





SPORTS

Lauren Betts isn’t looking for a break. Two weeks after her college season ended in April, she was drafted by the Mystics. Training camp started a few days later. Then, she played all 46 games of her rookie campaign. Two days after that season ended, she flew to Europe to spend the offseason playing for Turkish powerhouse Fenerbahçe. The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports that she is tired, sure — but she hopes the extra reps will help her develop as a player.

“I feel like I would be doing a disservice to myself if I didn’t just continue to grow,” she said.

Time is money: After parting ways with longtime coach Mike Locksley last week, the Maryland football program is getting creative in its attempts to fill SECU Stadium. The Diamondback reports that the school will be raffling off one semester of free tuition at Saturday’s home game against Illinois. The catch? Students have to stay until the fourth quarter to be eligible.

What to Watch Today

NBA: Wizards at Cavaliers, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

NHL: Capitals vs. Flyers, 7:30 p.m. (TNT)

MLS: D.C. United at Toronto, 7:30 p.m. (Apple TV)

entries.title: Morning Sun: Presidential Politicking
entries.content:
Today’s notice: 451 days until the first Democratic presidential primary. The latest from the 2026 map. A new poll finds Republicans don’t like how the federal government is being managed. A top Rubio aide quits. 





FROM 2028

Seven days from today the midterms will be in the past — and the starting gun for 2028 will have sounded. The Washington Sun’s Elena Schneider reports on how various Democratic factions are already scrambling to assemble their story of what happened in 2026 to influence what happens next. And that’s just the behind-the-scenes stuff. Would-be candidates have been building their name ID with appearances. And would-be would-be candidates are waiting to get elected.

“Everybody is going to look for a [2026] candidate to make their case for how they emulate that in 2028, whether it’s [Roy] Cooper in North Carolina, James Talarico in Texas, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, and say, ‘I’m like that person, I bring the same things to the table and I can win in these states,’” Morgan Jackson, a top adviser to Cooper’s Senate campaign, told Elena.

In New Mexico, they’re already ready for their new gig as fourth on the 2028 Democratic primary calendar. We took The Washington Sun Cast pod to the state for a weekend and ran into a passel of possible presidential nominees: Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Gov. Andy Beshear of Kentucky. We also ate everything in sight to try to get an answer to this elusive red- or green-chile question. Listen to our episode, featuring future major primary players including Sen. Ben Ray Luján, gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland and a mayor whose phone has not stopped ringing with calls from the aforementioned would-be presidents.

More: Ex-Biden Officials Want 2028 Democrats to Reject Biden and Trump Policies on Israel • Hasan Piker Hits Scott Jennings With a $72M Defamation Suit • House Democratic Whip Puts Her Money Where Her Mouth Is • Lawmakers’ Stock Selling Limited Their Exposure to Tariffs






THE MAP


Mississippi: No party-distancing for this Democrat. Senate nominee Scott Colom is running as a Democrat and standing next to as many Democrats as he can find — even in a state this red and this close to the election. We spent the day yesterday tagging along as he campaigned with potential 2028er Pete Buttigieg along the Gulf Coast. Even Colom’s GOTV signs at an extremely well-attended Biloxi rally were two shades of party blue.

In other red areas of the country, Democratic candidates have stayed as far away from the national party as possible. In South Carolina, for example, Senate nominee Annie Andrews has publicly said she doesn’t want any national Democrats to show up. But Colom has basically had them all, including Kamala Harris, who Mississippi rejected 61% to 38% in 2024. We asked Colom about his strategy: “Everybody I’m bringing out, we’re bringing attention to the issues that matter,” he told us. “And I appreciate them doing that because they know how important attention is in this moment.”

Kansas: Roger Marshall’s mayor says the senator is not a resident. “Look, it’s quite obvious he doesn’t live here anymore,” Great Bend’s mayor, Alan Moeder, told The Kansas City Star. “He lives in Florida. He has a little hunting lodge south of Great Bend in Stafford County. And I think that’s an issue for people, from what I hear.”

Nebraska: Another sleeper for Democrats? The Cook Political Report shifted the governor’s race from Likely to Lean Republican yesterday. It’s a four-way race: There’s a candidate running as more conservative than Republican Gov. Jim Pillen and one running on a pro-marijuana line to the left of Democratic nominee Lynne Walz. But Walz’s campaign tells The Sun it’s feeling momentum. Kansas Gov. Laura Kelly is coming to stump Friday — she’s a plains Democrat who upset a Republican, a move Team Walz says it can replicate.

Ohio: Still talking about Sen. Jon Husted’s butt. At a pair of events, Republicans almost uniformly made round-about references to his hind end. Among those were Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Sen. Bernie Moreno and CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz — the latter of whom told a crowd in Lima: “I’ve never gotten the compliments he’s received from the president, even though I’ve known the president for 20-something years.”

Husted couldn’t help but joke about it himself, telling supporters at an event earlier in the day in Clyde that with Donald Trump coming to the state on Wednesday, he’s had no choice but to hit the gym. “Don’t worry, I was in the weight room this morning,” Husted said to laughter. “I don’t let him down.”

Florida: Where gerrymandering looks like it could backfire. The 22nd District, a so-called “Frankenstein district,” was supposed to be a GOP-friendly blank slate stretching from the west sides of Palm Beach and Broward counties into Republican-leaning territory in more rural areas. But, The Sun’s Oriana González writes, the candidate Republicans picked to fill that blank slate, Casey Askar, seems to be, well, leaving it blank, ceding the public spaces to Democrat Pia Dandiya, a former educator and Apple lobbyist.

Colorado: MAGA star’s cakewalk is not so cakewalk-y. Rep. Lauren Boebert was seen as a lock in the 4th Congressional District, which had only elected one Democrat since the 1970s. But the race has become a target for Democrats, and Boebert’s Democratic opponent, Eileen Laubacher, has raised $13.7 million to the sitting congresswoman’s $1.2 million, The Washington Post reports.

Alaska: Lisa Murkowski out to prove her independent bona fides. The Republican senator, not up for reelection, endorsed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, calling him a “young Alaskan with a view and a perspective that I think Alaska needs right now,” KTUU reported. Murkowski has been critical of Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy.

Wisconsin: The STEM strategy’s race to watch. Keep an eye on the 1st District, where ER nurse Mitchell Berman is running against Republican Rep. Bryan Steil. In January, we told you about nascent efforts to recruit Democratic candidates with STEM backgrounds to run in flippable seats — the idea being that distaste with Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s HHS leadership could drive independents to cast pro-science votes. 314 Action Fund, the group behind the strategy, told The Sun’s Manuela Silva it has invested heavily in this race.

More: FEC Outage Hits One Week Out From Election Day


FROM THE WHITE HOUSE


Republican bureaucracy blues: Soon after Trump took office, some 69% of Republicans said the management of the federal government was headed in the right direction, a feeling that has now significantly soured. Only 47% say things are on the right track now, according to surveys commissioned by the Partnership for Public Service. Overall, Americans aren’t so happy: 63% say government management is headed in the “wrong direction,” with just 20% believing it’s on the right track.

More: Trump Gutted Refugee Programs. Those Already Here Feel Left Behind • Trump Unveils Plan to Relax Methane Emission Restrictions for Oil Companies 





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

A demolitionist’s exit: Jeremy Lewin, a top aide to Secretary of State Marco Rubio who helped decimate USAID, announced yesterday he was leaving the Trump administration — just hours after Wired reported he had not signed the paperwork usually required to work at USAID while he was gutting the agency.

A recently retired State Department official told The Sun’s Akbar Shahid Ahmed that they “despise” Lewin for what he did to USAID but said his departure does not suggest the administration might reassess its foreign-aid goals, since Lewin’s former portfolio is now held by State official Andrew Veprek, known for the policy of limiting U.S. refugee admissions to white South Africans.

NOT US

entries.title: The Midterms Are Almost Over. Democrats’ 2028 Jockeying Has Begun.
entries.summary: "The narrative battle is going to be ferocious for what 2026 means," said a Democratic strategist, and "everyone’s gearing up to fight that battle."
entries.content:
CEDAR RAPIDS, Iowa — In just a week, Democrats will know if they got their wave. The party’s many factions are not waiting to spin what the results will mean for the coming presidential race.

Third Way, a center-left organization, is polling voters this week on why they’re voting for — or against — Democrats and they’ll release the results immediately after Election Day, the group confirmed. They’ll also pop an analysis of all the TV ads that ran in battleground races. Searchlight, a Democratic think tank, will release policy white papers under the platform heading, “American Security Guarantee,” and the progressive Working Families Party will post its own pre- and postelection memos. Majority Democrats, Groundwork Action and Center for American Progress are all hosting splashy postelection confabs, featuring potential 2028 candidates, in early November.

The 2028 presidential campaigns-in-waiting are keeping meticulous track of what their candidates have done to help Democrats win, and they expect to push those talking points to allies and donors in the election’s immediate aftermath, according to two advisers to potential candidates who, like others quoted in this story, were granted anonymity to discuss private strategy and speak candidly.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

Even the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee prepared for 2028 this year. The committee sent memos to more than a dozen potential presidential candidates, hoping to direct them to districts aligned with their electoral strengths, according to two people directly familiar with the advice.

“You can’t swing a stick around these battleground states without running into a presidential candidate,” said Morgan Jackson, a top adviser to former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper (D), who is running for Senate in the state. “Everybody is going to look for a [2026] candidate to make their case for how they emulate that in 2028, whether it’s Cooper in North Carolina, James Talarico in Texas, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, and say, ‘I’m like that person, I bring the same things to the table and I can win in these states.’”

Tuesday’s midterms mark the official end of the Democratic presidential shadow primary that’s been simmering since President Donald Trump won his second term — and arguably since June 2024, after then-President Joe Biden’s disastrous debate. Interviews with more than a dozen strategists, lawmakers and advisers to the potential presidential campaigns said that the presidential primary functionally kicks off on Nov. 4. Different factions of the party, they said, will quickly begin to extract evidence from the midterms to prove their own theories for 2028 and jockey for standing with a new class of freshly elected Democratic stars. It’s bound to be messy, they said.

"The narrative battle is going to be ferocious for what 2026 means,” said a Democratic strategist, and “everyone’s gearing up to fight that battle.”

Four Democratic operatives said they expect at least one candidate to launch their presidential campaign before the end of the year. Many others, particularly those not currently in elected office, are expected to launch in early 2027, these operatives said.

The Democratic National Committee is expected to announce a framework for primary debates "earlier than ever," according to a person directly familiar with the committee's thinking. Ahead of the 2020 primary, the DNC announced debate thresholds and timing by late December of 2018.

Despite their rosy midterms polling, Democrats still face a serious brand problem. Approval of the Democratic Party is still underwater, even if voters prefer Democrats to Republicans. Four in 10 voters who are supporting Democrats this fall said the party doesn’t have a clear plan to fix the country’s economic woes, according to a CBS News poll released this past weekend. A majority of voters are backing Democrats to stop Trump, not for Democratic policies, the poll found.

“Rather than left, right, center, whatever ideological squabbles, we ought to be looking right up at the forces and the corrupt power that have made life worse for folks and be clear about what we’re going to do to fix it,” said Rep. Chris Deluzio, who stepped off the trail in his western Pennsylvania district on Tuesday for an interview.

Deluzio cited Democratic candidates Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania and Sam Forstag in Montana, both of whom picked up endorsements from the moderate Blue Dog Caucus and Sen. Bernie Sanders, as unifying examples of where “the party should go.”

Several strategists name-checked Michigan as a tell for Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez’s calculus and as a pressure spot for how both wings of the party will spin results. Earlier this month, the New York Democrat told donors that if Abdul El-Sayed, a firebrand progressive, can win a Senate seat in a purple state, then “anybody can win anywhere,” The New York Times reported.

“The corporate wing of the party has historically held a monopoly on swing districts and swing states, and they’ve manufactured this narrative that the left can’t compete in swing districts,” said Amirah Sequeria, director of federal affairs at the Working Families Party, which is boosting El-Sayed. “Anybody who is thinking about running for president will be seeing from this cycle that economic populism is resonating and future candidates who put forward a vision that speaks to economic populism will set themselves apart.”

For now, those future candidates are trying to set themselves apart through their midterm electioneering. Ocasio-Cortez has rallied for progressives in California, Florida and Michigan. Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker gave $40 million to Democratic candidates. Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly campaigned in 23 states this year. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear led the Democratic Governors Association with 39 races on the ballot. Pete Buttigieg stumped for 60 candidates over the last year, and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock fought to get the Mississippi Senate race onto the Democratic map. Several potential candidates, including Maryland Gov. Wes Moore and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, were up for reelection themselves and primarily stumped for candidates in their own states.

All that cash and campaigning could help birth a new class of Democratic stars whose “phone lines will be lighting up” the moment they win, an adviser to a presidential candidate said. “Everyone wants to be seen standing next to James Talarico.”
AP26279161058662 (4000x2667, AR: 1.50)The early contours of what voters want from future presidential candidates is already coming into view in places like Iowa, where Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek is challenging Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) in the Senate race.

After a canvass launch last weekend, Turek assured a pair of Iron Workers Union members lingering inside an IBEW hall that he wasn’t “out there talking about culture war issues.” He was focused instead, he said, on Iowans’ economic concerns. The union workers nodded along vigorously.

Those union members — Brandon Winders, an independent, and Isabelle Hoffman, who said she “leans conservative” — said it’s a challenge to convince their friends it’s worth voting these days, as they are turned off by the relentless negativity on TV. “Most people sort of gave up” on voting, Hoffman said, “because nothing changes.”

Turek said in an interview with The Washington Sun that Democrats have “quite possibly” talked too much about culture war issues in recent years — and he hopes the 2028 Democrats take notice.

“If we do, I think we'll win a lot more elections,” he said, “and that doesn't matter if you're in New York City or in Council Bluffs, Iowa.”

During his campaign, Turek stumped alongside two potential contenders: Kelly and Buttigieg, who endorsed Turek during his contentious primary.

Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate for governor in Iowa, has largely avoided national Democrats this cycle, as he tries to shake loose of partisan labels altogether — though he will be campaigning alongside Beshear this weekend. Sand told volunteers in Cedar Rapids last weekend that Iowa’s “always been a state that doesn’t shout about being red or blue,” nor is it about “being Democratic or Republican, but making government work for ordinary people.”

When pressed by The Sun on his advice for Democrats, Sand was reluctant to dole out any. But he’s made clear that he has put himself in position to win his race by going “everywhere” and “talking to everybody,” including in the “out-of-the-way places that are just as important as Des Moines.” Sand noted he’s the only Democrat to do a 99-county tour of the state annually.

Sand, who has stirred presidential interest of his own among some Democratic operatives, did go so far as to identify what he thought voters might be looking for in leaders: “There are plenty of people who are looking for someone who's outside of the political structure because they're so disappointed with the political structure.”

“But at the same time, when they find someone who's doing what I'm doing the way I'm doing it,” Sand continued, “they'll say, ‘No, that's great,’ because you might know how some of this stuff works, but also you're willing to, you know, do it differently.”

entries.title: D.C.’s Biggest Election Debate: Should Foie Gras Be Banned?
entries.summary: Star chefs and social media users are hotly debating a ballot initiative that would ban the sale of foods that result from the force-feeding of fowl.
entries.content:
These days chef José Andrés is best known for his humanitarian work across the globe, but last week he dove into a political and culinary issue now facing D.C., the city where he opened his first restaurant more than three decades ago.

“So we are banning all meats? If Duck goes all goes next?” he wrote on X to his 1.1 million followers, encouraging people to “concentrate on things that matter.”

Andrés was criticizing Initiative 86, the D.C. ballot measure that seeks to ban the production and sale of foods that result from the force-feeding of fowl — largely foie gras, the French delicacy that comes from the fattened livers of ducks and geese.

“Yes let’s bring the ducks now,” Andrés wrote. “... one more issue for restaurants to handle!”

The ballot initiative has been quietly floating through D.C.’s political process for the better part of a year. The Washington Sun first reported on it in June, in a story featuring a politically engaged (and likely self-interested) duck. But with ballots having been mailed to every registered voter and the Nov. 3 election less than a week off, the question is now directly facing the city’s residents — many of whom may be saying, “Qu'est-ce que c'est?”
Meghan Abrego gathers signatures to ban foie gras at Eastern Market alongside her duck Olivia Gray. (7921x5281, AR: 1.50)The initiative has also thrown D.C.’s restaurateurs into a political and ethical debate they may not want to have right now, especially as the city’s hospitality industry struggles to survive an economic slump, and individual chefs may be hesitant to make their opinions known for fear of social media backlash.

“I don’t really like foie gras, but I do think restaurants should have the right to serve it,” said Geoff Tracy, the owner of Chef Geoff’s. “It’s one additional regulation or one more thing we have to deal with. Just leave us alone for a little bit. This is a nothing burger, but you still have to push back and say, ‘Enough is enough.’”

The ballot initiative has been spearheaded by Pro-Animal Future D.C., a local chapter of a Colorado-based animal rights group that has pushed similar efforts in Portland and Denver, where voters will also be deciding the issue next week. (Foie gras has been partially banned in California, and its production is restricted in many European countries.)

Its volunteer and paid petition circulators worked through the earlier part of the year collecting signatures to get Initiative 86 on the ballot; they submitted some 31,000 signatures to the city’s elections board over the summer, qualifying the initiative for the November ballot.

The group says it targeted D.C. both because it allows ballot initiatives and because, for as niche a product as foie gras may be, it is available in a number of restaurants in the city. “D.C. is the third top consumer of foie gras, so getting rid of it would have a big impact on the foie gras industry,” said Natalie Fulton, a spokesperson for Pro-Animal Future.

That industry, she added, is particularly inhumane. “Factory farming is cruel, but foie gras farms are uniquely cruel because ducks are force fed,” she said. The campaign has leaned heavily into this, including imagery of ducks with feeding tubes down their throats.

For some voters, the campaign has been convincing.

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

“I voted for it because it seems inhumane to me and unfair to the ducks,” said David Abramson, a Ward 1 voter who cast a ballot on Monday in Columbia Heights. “There’s always a balance between regulation and freedom to engage in these things. In the same way that there are laws about abuse of pets and other animals, I feel the same should apply here.”

Michael Votta, who emerged from the same early-voting center only minutes later, saw it differently. “It’s not really the government’s business,” he said. “If somebody wants to farm more sustainably or less sustainably, I would rather that be left to the consumer rather than be legislated.”

That’s the position taken by Bart Hutchins, a co-owner of the buzzy Capitol Hill restaurant Butterworth’s, who serves foie gras on his menu. (Andrés also offers Cotton Candy Foie Gras on the menu of The Bazaar at the Waldorf Astoria.) He argues that not only is the production not as harmful to ducks as critics claim, but that targeting foie gras ignores more significant issues with factory-farmed meats that are eaten by far more Americans.

“Commercial pigs are disgusting. Commercial chickens, too,” Hutchins told The Sun this summer. “We could ban the sales of animals raised that way, or there are many ways we could be conscious of animals and the quality of our foods, but this isn’t one.”
Butterworth Foie Gras (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)Leah Curran Moon and Michael Jantz Moon, owners of the DC Vegan restaurant, take issue with Hutchins’ advocacy for foie gras. “No dish is worth this level of cruelty,” they wrote in a statement. “Chefs around the world proudly serve exceptional cuisine without foie gras, proving that compassion and culinary excellence belong on the same plate.”

James Nance agrees. The D.C.-based lawyer is also a very specific type of food influencer; to his more than 42,000 followers, he’s just D.C. Carnivores. “I don’t like factory farming, but it’s going to be here,” he told The Sun. “I separate that from foie gras because foie gras seems very unnecessary.”

Geoff Tracy and other critics of Initiative 86 say it’s about more than just foie gras; it’s about who gets to tell restaurants what they can and can’t do. Over the past decade, the tipped minimum wage that restaurants have long used became a central topic of debate, resulting in two separate ballot initiatives aiming to eliminate it, and a third potentially coming in the next year.

“I think the District is just such an easy place for outside agencies to get something on a ballot and have it impact the city,” Tracy said. “The question is: Do the voters really want to be weighing in on this? It’s so out of left field.”

That’s where outgoing Mayor Muriel Bowser seems to fall in the debate over whether foie gras should be banned. “I have an issue with national issues being dumped on D.C. residents, and I think this may be one such issue,” she told The Sun this week, referring to the significant amount of out-of-state money — more than $350,000 — that fueled the anti-foie gras campaign. “That should give you some hint where I’m going.”

Fulton of Pro-Animal Future disagrees that Initiative 86 is some out-of-left-field issue pushed by out-of-towners. “We have hundreds of local D.C. people working on this,” she said, citing local protests that flared up outside restaurants that serve foie gras.

Ahead of next week’s election, Hutchins isn’t ducking the issue — in fact, he’s leaning into it. This week Butterworth’s is hosting “Foie Gras At The End Of The World: A Tasting Menu,” which Hutchins calls a “four-course send-off” for foie gras. The proceeds will also go toward an eventual defense fund for any restaurants that could be fined up to $5,000 for serving foie gras, should Initiative 86 be approved by voters and implemented by the D.C. Council.

“Sometimes you have to push back on the ridiculousness,” Tracy said.

entries.title: Trump Gutted Refugee Programs. Those Already Here Feel Left Behind.
entries.summary: Refugee communities are losing access to services that helped them integrate.
entries.content:
Two years after arriving in the United States and 12 years after fleeing her native Somalia and arriving at an Ethiopian refugee camp, 80-year-old Hawo Jimale says she is struggling to afford her medicine and groceries.

Under a measure President Donald Trump signed into law last year, Jimale, like most newly arriving refugees, lost access to her federal food assistance. Under another Trump directive implemented earlier this month, she lost access to Medicaid.

Jimale, who has trouble moving around on her own and spends most of her time alone in her Columbus, Ohio, apartment, worries that next she will lose her Social Security benefits, her only source of income and the only way she can afford her rent.

Her social life has taken a hit, too. The Trump administration has terminated the Services to Older Refugees program that, through a local nonprofit, funded social events for seniors, such as a trip to the zoo. Jimale said she now questions whether she has done something wrong.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

“Why did they bring me here if they don’t help me?” Jimale asked through an interpreter.

The Trump administration formally rescinded money from the office carrying out refugee support programs at the end of September through pocket rescissions, a controversial budgetary maneuver that the government’s spending watchdog has deemed illegal. Overall spending on refugee support services has been cut by 80% since former President Joe Biden’s final year in office. Last fiscal year, the government spent $132 million on the now-eliminated programs focusing on students, mentorship, older refugees and health promotion.

“It came like a flash flood, without any warning,” said Jhuma Acharya, the family engagement and support coordinator for the Licking Heights school district just outside of Columbus.

The federal cuts to refugee programs have been devastating to families in his communities, Acharya said. “Without any announcement it comes, and then everyone is uprooted.”

Central Ohio has become a flash point in the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to restricting immigration, particularly after Vice President JD Vance accused Haitian immigrants in Springfield of eating pets. Ohio was accepting among the most refugees of any state before the administration decimated those efforts and began welcoming only white South Africans. Officials across the region now fear they will no longer have the resources to support the communities that have already arrived or integrate them into American society.

“Columbus has long been a resettlement city,” Lourdes Barroso de Padilla, a council member for the city, told The Washington Sun. The cuts to federal funding are making it “challenging to provide those other things that create that sense of belonging,” she said.

Acharya said families in his district took advantage of local organizations that offered federally funded youth mentorship, through which individuals would help refugee students with integration and educational goals.

“These kids are living in two different cultural worlds every day,” said Acharya, himself a refugee from Bhutan who arrived in the United States in 2011 after spending 19 years in a Nepalese camp. “They have to shift their brains two to three times per day.”

The mentors helped students perform those mental gymnastics, develop their language skills and navigate various bureaucratic processes.

Angie Plummer, executive director of Community Refugee and Immigration Services Ohio, the organization that led Jimale’s outings, said her organization has gone through “massive layoffs” since the start of Trump’s second term as federal funding has continued to dry up, which she said has had cascading fallout for the families it supports.

“They’ve been building up trust with the families,” Plummer said of the case workers she used to employ. Increasingly, she said, refugees are “left on their own to navigate all these systems.”

One former official in the Office of Refugee Resettlement said the agency’s spending enabled psychosocial adjustments for children who had experienced trauma.

“These are kids who may have witnessed their parents being killed in front of them,” the former official said, adding that ORR-backed programs helped children learn and achieve in the classroom. “All of that is gone now.”

The former official said that in years past, as the number of incoming refugees ebbed and flowed, funding would be reallocated to existing populations.

“Someone who arrived at age six and is now in third grade, they’re still leaning on things,” they said. “The trauma doesn’t go away in a year.”

A spokesperson for the Health and Human Services Department, which houses the Office of Refugee Resettlement that funded the canceled programs, said the agency will continue directing “available resources toward families and older refugees with the greatest needs.”

“ORR remains committed to this mission and works with states, resettlement agencies and communities to make effective use of available resources,” the spokesperson said. “ORR regularly reviews priorities, assesses needs and manages taxpayer dollars responsibly, while prioritizing entitlement spending for American citizens.”

In clawing back money for refugees this year, the White House said the ORR programs were “operated by pro-illegal immigration non-profits” and eliminating them would support the administration’s goal of “ending the use of federal taxpayer dollars to support non-citizens, putting Americans first.”

Tom Betti, a spokesman for Ohio’s Department of Job and Family Services, said the state continues to receive funding for the federal refugee employment program and is “awaiting federal guidance on how states may use” existing funding set aside for students and older refugees.

Barroso de Padilla, the City Council member and a daughter of Cuban refugees, said the program cuts will impact the entire region.

“The number one thing behind our population growth is immigrants and refugees,” she said. “They’re helping to shape our cities, helping to shape our cultural scene, helping to shape our entrepreneurial scene.”

Those contributions are part of what motivates people to want to live in and around Columbus, she said. The waning federal support is forcing Columbus to make tough choices.

“When the federal government doesn’t do its job, when the state government doesn't do its job, then it’s imperative for us to do that,” Barroso de Padilla said. “We are the last line of defense.”

Nirere Dancille arrived in the Columbus area recently with her daughter and granddaughter after fleeing war in their native Democratic Republic of the Congo.

She did not speak English and leaned on federally funded groups to make and get to medical appointments, find housing, put her grandchild in school, learn the language and go to events with other seniors.

“We feel home here now,” Dancille said through an interpreter. “We feel home because we feel peaceful and safe.”

Still, like Jimale, feelings of loneliness and isolation — and concern for how they will pay for their next meals or dose of medicine — have settled in.

Before the funding was cut off, Dancille traveled with other older refugees to an American history museum.

“We could not imagine the history of America,” she said. “We learned many things that helped us compare where we are to our homes.”

Plummer said her group has focused on helping refugees develop that sense of belonging. But without federal funding, she said, her organization will no longer be able to put on events like taking refugee seniors to a local park to play cornhole.

“All these Congolese people were doing a very American activity,” Plummer said.

entries.title: Republicans Made This Florida District Red. Their Candidate May Keep It Blue.
entries.summary: The race for the redrawn 22nd District is a toss-up and the GOP nominee is hardly anywhere to be seen.
entries.content:
PLANTATION, Fla. — Republican U.S. House candidate Casey Askar, a pizza maven and entrepreneur, lives about a 5 mile drive from the district where he is running, one of four that the Florida state GOP redrew to favor their party.

His home is an extravagant mansion where he cannot be seen, isolated behind a massive gatehouse. The residence could serve as something of a metaphor for his campaign for Florida’s 22nd Congressional District, where he also is not especially visible, has spent a lot of his own money and still might lose to his Democratic opponent, Pia Dandiya.

“I haven’t seen him around here at all,” said Republican Florida state Rep. Anne Gerwig. She represents Wellington, one of the largest municipalities in Palm Beach County, one of four counties encompassed by the 22nd District.

The new district map that Republicans crafted got rid of one of the largest Democratic seats in South Florida, the 20th Congressional District. The majority-Black seat was represented by former Rep. Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick and created in 1992 by a federal court as a remedy for racial exclusion. It is one of the four GOP-leaning seats that Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis enacted in May, along with those held by Democratic Reps. Kathy Castor, Jared Moskowitz and Darren Soto.

On the cusp of the midterm elections, the partisan gerrymandering looks like it may have backfired, with just Soto’s 9th District considered likely to fall to Republicans by the prognosticator Cook Political Report.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

Castor and Moskowitz may overcome the unfavorable maps thanks to souring prospects for the president’s party and the advantages of incumbency. But the 22nd District, a so-called “Frankenstein district,” was supposed to be a GOP-friendly blank slate stretching from the west sides of Palm Beach and Broward counties into Republican-leaning territory in more rural areas and into Hendry County and southern Collier County.

Askar seemed to be a good fit. An Iraqi immigrant whose legal name is Kousay Askar, he paints himself as a product of the American dream: A Medium post he wrote says his family immigrated to the U.S. to escape religious persecution, he enlisted in the U.S. Marines after graduating high school, and ultimately became a businessman and restaurant franchise owner. According to his financial disclosures, his net worth ranges anywhere between $97.5 million and $480.5 million.

The district that Republicans created has more registered Republicans than Democrats, and President Donald Trump would have won it in 2024 by 11 points.

What looks good on the surface, however, doesn’t always translate. When the Cook Political Report moved the race from “lean Republican” to “toss-up” in September, the analysts pointed out Trump would have lost it by three points in 2020. And 2026 is looking a lot more like that year.

Then there’s the problem of Askar’s campaign style. The candidate Republicans picked to fill that blank slate seems to be, well, leaving it blank, ceding the public spaces to Dandiya, a former educator and Apple lobbyist.
DANDIYA (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)DANDIYA (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)For instance, Gerwig told The Washington Sun that her friends in the area have yard signs for Dandiya “at their homes” in the eastern side of the district. Asked whether she had seen any signs for Askar, she said, “I haven’t seen them around here.”

Dave Shepard, a resident of Marco Island south of Naples, a Republican stronghold on the western side of the district, said he votes for Republicans “most of the time” but that he could not name Askar “off hand.” He told The Sun he had seen plenty of political yard signs for city council races but hadn’t noticed any for Askar. None of the voters interviewed for this story said they had attended or seen an Askar campaign event in their community.

Askar also does not appear to have a headquarters for his campaign, with the only physical address available on public records being a UPS Store P.O. Box in Naples outside of the district, about a 10 minute drive from Askar’s house in Naples’ Port Royal neighborhood.

No one appeared to be home when a Sun reporter went to Askar’s house, and he did not respond to a note left in his mailbox after multiple attempts to reach him by phone and email.

While Askar has been pictured at some local events, some only for registered Republicans, there are no public ones listed on his campaign website. The Florida Republican Party and the four Republican county parties in the district did not have any events with Askar in the last week before the election, and a website listing events in Southeast Florida did not show anything with Askar. 

Republican Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart, whose district lost portions to the 22nd District, told the Sun he has run into Askar at different events in Broward County, saying that “he is working.”

One Democratic operative, who was granted anonymity to talk about campaign opposition research strategy, told The Sun that even political trackers paid to trail candidates are having a hard time finding Askar because of his lack of public appearances.

The campaign knows it has a problem, at least judging by what the candidate has said out of sight. In an audio recording obtained by The Sun from a mid-October voter meet and greet in Broward County organized by a local Republican group, Askar said that an internal poll conducted with the National Republican Campaign Committee against Dandiya found him “down about five and a quarter points.”

“Don’t be afraid of this,” Askar told attendees, before introducing the poll. The Sun did not review the poll Askar mentioned.

Republicans have not released any polling on the race, but House Majority PAC, the flagship House Democratic super PAC, found Dandiya leading Askar by two percentage points in a head-to-head matchup in a September poll.

The NRCC did not answer questions about polling, instead ripping Dandiya as a “radical Democrat” who will be rejected by voters.

What Askar is doing is dumping money into TV advertising in the general election: over $2 million, according to campaign records. Dandiya has spent $2.2 million for TV advertising, according to campaign records. The race is the third-most expensive House race in Florida. Outside groups are also spending heavily.
DANDIYA (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)An air war in the sprawling district does make sense, said Michael Worley, a Democratic strategist and CEO of the Florida-based political and public affairs firm MDW Communications, which is working with Dandiya’s campaign. “TV has to be the most effective” way to campaign across the district’s three large and expensive media markets: Fort Myers, West Palm Beach and Miami.

One Florida Republican operative, also granted anonymity to speak about Askar’s presence, said that his campaign also has flooded the strongly Republican Naples area with mailers and text messages, but he has not held any rallies.

Askar’s physical absence and media shyness is costing him more than local recognition.

Michael Napoleone, the Republican mayor of Wellington, broke with his party and endorsed Dandiya. He said part of the reason he did so was because Askar has refused to respond to news outlets’ requests for comments and interviews.

It “is very telling to me sometimes because more and more often, certain people, they just don’t want to respond to valid questions that voters want to know the answer to,” Napoleone said. “That does a disservice to the voters if you're not willing to sit down and answer what might be hard or uncomfortable questions.”

Worley argued a campaign that relies mainly on television advertising without a ground game, “90% of the time, that does not work.” He pointed to Democrat Jeff Greene’s 2018 governor race, whose campaign prioritized media advertising over on-the-ground efforts. He finished fourth in the Democratic primary.

Like Greene, Askar is also a largely self-funded candidate: He has loaned his campaign over $6.6 million, about $3.5 million just in the general election.

Most of Askar’s TV ads, as well as those from outside groups, have focused on attacking Dandiya. They appear to have helped the Democrat’s name recognition rather than his own. The Sun spoke to 28 voters in Marco Island, most of whom said they did not remember Askar’s name. They still planned to vote Republican. One voter who declined to be named, for example, said, “I know not Pia,” when asked who they’d be supporting in the race.

Dandiya, who also lives outside of the district, has been trying to fill the hole left by Askar, holding many more events and out-raising him significantly through traditional fundraising. In the third quarter, Dandiya hauled in more than $1.3 million compared to $321,000 for Askar.

Dandiya said that she has done over 70 meet and greets with voters “and I am so grateful to have met those folks in the community and to understand their needs.”
DANDIYA (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)DANDIYA (5000x3333, AR: 1.50)“That's been essential because how are we going to know what to fix and how to fix it if we're not talking to people and listening to people?” she added. “My opponent has not been very visible in the district. … That seems to be the theme of his campaign, that he wants to not really be a representative; he wants to be a rubber stamp for Trump.”

Dandiya held a rally Monday in Plantation with former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, a potential presidential candidate in 2028. He’s one of multiple Democratic surrogates that have traveled to the district, including potential 2028 contender Rahm Emanuel and Reps. Jamie Raskin and Suzan DelBene, the chair of House Democrats’ campaign arm.

Democrats say they are feeling bullish about their chances in the district, even with redistricting.

“This district was drawn specifically in order to give an unfair advantage to Republicans,” Buttigieg said. “Instead of trying to persuade the voters, their strategy is to rearrange the voters so that they can pick their voters instead of the other way around. But I think we’re going to win anyways and when we do it, it will send a very powerful message out to those guys.”

“Think about the shock waves that will radiate through this country when we win in this district,” he added.

Trump held a rally in the neighboring district to boost GOP turnout in the state last Friday.

Askar wasn’t visible there, either.

entries.title: Lawmakers’ Stock Selling Limited Their Exposure to Tariffs
entries.summary: Many Republican lawmakers have publicly supported Trump’s tariff regime.
entries.content:
Members of Congress sold off millions of dollars in shares of companies exposed to President Donald Trump’s tariffs this year, even as they publicly downplayed, praised or voted against ending the policies.

Republicans and Democrats alike have mitigated their tariff exposure by shedding the stocks of companies operating supply chains vulnerable to Trump’s policies, from semiconductor manufacturers to clothing retailers, according to an analysis of congressional financial disclosures by The Washington Sun.

Many of the lawmakers told The Sun that they do not control their own stock sales and purchases, but rather use independent outside financial advisers for any trades. Those advisers have routinely acted on behalf of their congressional clients in a way that shows the economic reality of tariffs differently from what Republicans have publicly insisted.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

The trades show the extent that Trump’s ever-changing tariff regime has impacted the economy and the finances of even his defenders. The president’s policies have saturated many sectors of the U.S. economy, sparing few companies and driving prices higher for both business owners trying to make ends meet and consumers frustrated by the rising cost of living.

In some cases, many of the stocks lawmakers replaced previous holdings with carried their own significant tariff exposure.

Rep. Tony Wied (R-Wisconsin) dropped at least between $395,000 and $950,000 in tariff-exposed stocks this year. The majority came from companies that manufacture semiconductors or related equipment, including at least $150,001 in Lam Research and $100,001 in Advanced Micro Devices stock. The transactions were made through a jointly owned account.

In January, Trump levied 25% tariffs on the semiconductor industry and is reportedly considering enforcing new semiconductor tariffs. Wied sold the affected Lam Research stocks during a nine-day period in February. Lawmakers are only required to report the value of their transactions in broad ranges.

"I think he’s doing the right thing, utilizing different tools to be able to use those tariffs, again, as leverage to do what’s best for our country, and to grow our economy and make us safer and more secure,” Wied told C-SPAN in February, weeks after selling semiconductor industry stocks.

"Rep. Wied has zero involvement in his stock trading. All of his investments are managed solely through an independent financial advisor, and he has no role in any of their decisions,” his spokesperson Aidan Strongreen said in a statement to The Sun.

Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama) dumped at least between $47,000 and $180,000 in tariff-exposed stocks over a couple days in June, the Sun’s analysis found. Most of those transactions were made through a jointly owned account. The husband of Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-West Virginia) sold at least between $7,000 and $105,000 of his own tariff-exposed stocks this year, including Broadcom, Intel and Apple shares.

The Republican lawmakers publicly defended the president’s tariffs, acknowledging their strain on the U.S. economy while justifying those financial pressures.

“You know, we’re going to have some short-term pain for long-term gain,” Tuberville told Fox News in April 2025, adding that the president is “gonna do whatever it takes to usher in a Golden Age for the American economy.”

Moore Capito has said tariffs are a “negotiating item for” the president that could lead to a “more fair deal” for workers, though she has acknowledged that “there is pain associated with” tariffs.

“The uncertainty of this is starting to wear on people, particularly with supply chains, but I think they’re willing to ride it out with the president,” Moore Capito told reporters in July of last year.

Moore Capito and Tuberville did not respond to requests for comment.

The Sun used the financial disclosures of some of Congress’ highest volume stock traders to identify transactions involving companies with supply chains vulnerable to Trump’s tariffs. The Sun confirmed each company’s tariff exposure using quarterly earnings reports and Securities and Exchange Commission filings.

A majority of Americans believe Trump’s tariff policies will have a mostly negative impact on the country, and the share of Republicans feeling optimistic about them has fallen to a minority, according to a Pew Research Center poll published earlier this month.

A Federal Reserve Bank of New York study released in August found that 26% of the 2025 tariff hikes pass through to the prices consumers pay.

Many lawmakers and their family members are limiting the impact of tariffs on their own stock portfolios.

Rep. Michael McCaul’s (R-Texas) wife sold between at least $1.07 million and $3.24 million in tariff-exposed stocks from January to June of this year, though he purchased a similar dollar range of such stocks. In April 2025, Linda Mays McCaul sold at least between $265,000 and $650,000 in stocks over a more than six-week period following the April 2 tariff announcement, including at least between $200,002 and $500,000 worth of shares in Kraft Heinz, which faced tariffs on a slew of imported ingredients. Mays McCaul sold at least between $100,001 and $250,000 of those Kraft Heinz shares on the same day as the announcement.

"Congressman McCaul did not purchase these stocks. Rather, his wife has assets she solely owns, and a third-party manager made the purchase without her direction,” McCaul’s attorney Elliot Berke said in a statement to The Sun.

The wife of Rep. Dan Newhouse (R-Washington), who voted to eliminate tariffs on Canada, sold at least between $9,000 and $135,000 in tariff-exposed stocks on a single day in July, though she purchased a slightly lower range — $7,000 to $105,000 — in similar stocks on the same day.

“Neither Congressman Newhouse nor his wife have any involvement in the stock transactions in their portfolio,” a spokesperson for Newhouse said. “Their financial advisor handles all transactions and required reporting.”

Accounts tied to Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R-New Jersey) offloaded at least between $90,000 and $475,000 of tariff-exposed stocks between January and August. Half of the sales took place during Kean’s absence from Congress earlier this year, The Sun previously reported. Kean has previously said that he has no influence over the individual investment decisions of his outside financial advisers and has backed legislation banning lawmakers from purchasing individual stocks.

Some of Congress’s most prolific stock traders have cooled their high-volume stock trading this year following press coverage of their previous transactions, according to The Sun’s review of publicly available financial disclosures. A spokesperson for Rep. Julie Johnson (D-Texas) — who made 77 stock sales the day before “Liberation Day” and dozens more after — told The Sun last month that Johnson would stop trading individual stocks.

Freshman Rep. Jefferson Shreve (R-Indiana) sold at least between $1.47 million and $3.8 million in tariff-exposed stocks between February and May 2025, including hundreds of thousands of dollars in Amazon, Costco and Walmart stock, according to a new Washington Sun analysis. The Sun previously reported that Shreve — one of Congress’s wealthiest members — made more than 140 individual stock purchases and sales totaling at least between $3.44 million and $9.45 million during a 10-day stretch in April 2025. A spokesperson for Shreve told The Sun in December he would quit individual stock trading.

A spokesperson for Shreve told The Sun the transactions are unrelated to tariffs and reflect when Shreve directed the asset manager of his charitable trust to divest from individual stocks.

“Mr. Shreve has not traded personally-held stocks as a member of Congress and has voted to ban Congressional stock trading,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pennsylvania), whose median net worth is $34 million, dumped stocks worth at least between $74,000 and $935,000 in companies vulnerable to Trump’s tariffs in late March and April 2025, The Sun found.

Bresnahan and Shreve have both said they rely on outside financial advisers to manage their wealth. However, transactions in both lawmakers’ portfolios have slowed this year, amounting to just $166,000 to $365,000 in purchases by Bresnahan of index funds, bonds and securities. Shreve sold at least between $10,000,002 and $50 million in annuities and purchased $29 million to $145 million in annuities and structured notes tied to equity indices like the S&P 500.

In July, the House passed a bill — the Stop Insider Trading Act — to ban congressional stock buying. But despite most Americans supporting a congressional stock-trade ban and the issue becoming a major campaign issue, the bill died in the Senate last month. Democrats blocked it because many considered it rife with loopholes and had been tethered to an unrelated national voter identification measure. Some lawmakers are vowing to try again during the post-election lame duck congressional session or next year with a new Congress.
