entries.title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Oct. 29)
entries.summary: Go-go with the Washington Ballet, cheer on Charo and dance at dueling Día de los Muertos parties.
entries.content:
Thursday

D.C. By Foot: Ghosts of Georgetown and Exorcist Steps Walking Tour

3051 M St. NW (Old Stone House), 7 p.m. and 8 p.m., $49

Spooky season is an opportune time to play tourist in your own town. Learn some history, listen for the screams of Civil War amputees and end your night at the steps featured in the 1973 film.

“Beatrice Likes the Dark” closes at Adventure Theatre MTC

7300 MacArthur Boulevard, Glen Echo, 11 a.m., $27

Local playwright and actor Dani Stoller adapted the popular children’s book about an amateur spellcaster for Adventure Theatre MTC, the youth playhouse at Glen Echo Park. Performances continue through Sunday and are aimed at brave children 5 and up.

More to explore: New England folk rockers Griffin William Sherry and Jesse James DeConto at Pie Shop

Friday

Charo at Montgomery College’s Cultural Art Center

7995 Georgia Avenue, Silver Spring, 7:30 p.m., $35-80 

It’s entirely possible that you know who Charo is without knowing what she’s famous for. The Spanish actress, singer and comedian was a queen of ’60s and ’70s American television, appearing on “Laugh-In,” “Fantasy Island” and other shows. But she was a flamenco artist first and will have a guitar in hand for this show aimed at nostalgic TV watchers and queer fans way too young to have seen her on the Johnny Carson show.

The Washington Ballet’s Go-Go 50 at the Warner Theatre

513 13th St. NW, 7:30, $166 to $202

Singaporean choreographer Choo San Goh helped put the Washington Ballet on the map when he became the company’s resident choreographer in the 1980s. This weekend, the company celebrates 50 years of dancing in the District by performing Goh’s 1981 classic “Configurations,” as well as a piece by current artistic director Edwaard Liang and a new ballet set to go-go music by choreographer Chanel DaSilva. The program continues through Sunday; best seating availability is Saturday night.

More to explore: Classical Arts Society of Washington presents “The Devil’s Trill” 

Saturday

Dupont Fall Festival, Pumpkin Patch and Bluegrass Jamboree

Dupont Circle, 1 to 4 p.m., free

The fifth Dupont Circle fall fête gives city dwellers a strong incentive to don their costumes early. Winners in the adult, kid and pet categories will each take home a $100 gift certificate good at Dupont-area restaurants. Plus everyone gets a pumpkin (while supplies last) to decorate while Shannon Leigh and the Good Bygones play bluegrass.

The Miss Adams Morgan Pageant at the Washington Hilton

1919 Connecticut Avenue NW, 8 p.m., $25 cocktail party, $100 for the whole evening

Mirror, mirror on the hotel ballroom wall, who’s the fairest drag queen of them all? Since 1988, the Dupont Social Club has celebrated queer rights with an annual drag contest where both the contestants and the audience are invited to come in costume.

More to explore: ’80s Mayhem Halloween Dance Party at the Black Cat

Sunday

Día de los Muertos Celebration at The Wharf

M Street Landing SW, 3 to 6:30 p.m., free

Since 2019, The Wharf has become the District’s place to see and be seen with dancing skeletons, elaborate Catrina flower crowns and mariachi bands. The Day of the Dead celebration features two stages: one for music and one for folklorica dance troupes, plus a kids’ pier with sugar-skull painting and snacks. The revelry begins at 3 p.m. and concludes with a candlelight procession.

Día de los Muertos Celebration at MOCA Arlington 

3550 Wilson Blvd., Arlington, 5 to 8 p.m., free

On the Virginia side of the Potomac, Arlington’s Museum of Contemporary Art is hosting an evening picnic. Bring your own dinner, or buy tacos from on-site vendors. Music begins at 5:30 p.m., there’s a Catrina parade at 6:20 p.m. and crafts for kids all night long. All attendees are invited to bring a deceased loved one’s photo and contribute to an altar created by Arlington artist David Amoroso.

More to explore: Violinist Daniel Hope plays music of the Gilded Age at The Barns at Wolf Trap.

entries.title: House Democratic Whip Puts Her Money Where Her Mouth Is
entries.summary: Rep. Katherine Clark spearheads the party's affordability push while raising tons of cash.
entries.content:
House Minority Whip Katherine Clark has raised $50 million this election cycle, cementing her reputation as a top fundraiser as Democrats eye retaking the majority — a victory that would position the Massachusetts lawmaker as the first woman to serve as majority leader.

Clark’s fundraising haul represents a nearly 43% increase from the $35 million she raised in 2024, according to figures shared with The Washington Sun from campaign operatives that include direct giving, fundraising for several entities supporting Democratic incumbents and challengers, and events co-hosted for candidates.

But this slate of Democratic leaders faces pressure to step up their fundraising at a time when financial resources can be a major factor in determining who has the majority. The leadership team, led by Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, faces a formidable task of filling the shoes of their predecessors, including former Speaker Rep. Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring. Pelosi’s extensive donor network and fundraising prowess was the backbone of House Democrats’ political operations for two decades.

According to a breakdown of donations provided to The Sun by Clark’s team, the No. 2 Democrat gave to a range of entities. She helped raise or donate over $25 million to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, over $10 million to Frontline and Red to Blue candidates and nearly $13 million to House Democrats facing competitive races. In some cases, she co-hosted fundraisers with other Democrats.

Clark’s significant uptick in racking up donations coincides with historically large spending by Democrats and Republicans on competitive races. Jeffries’ affiliated House Majority PAC and House Majority Forward raised over $548 million combined through the third quarter of 2026. The House Majority PAC raised $44 million in the first two weeks of October.

The ability to dole out money to colleagues and incoming members can help leaders build relationships across the caucus, especially with vulnerable members.

Brendan Glavin, director of research for the nonprofit OpenSecrets, stressed the need for members in leadership roles to “deliver money to the party so that then they can divvy that money out where it's needed around the country.”

As whip, Clark has become known for cultivating relationships with incoming freshmen, serving as a mentor to many and earning a reputation as someone who checks in regularly on topics unrelated to a vote count.

During the political season, she has criss-crossed the country focused on Democrats’ affordability messaging.

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read.

Clark is scheduled to visit seven states this month, including Pennsylvania this week. In early October, she visited Ohio, where she campaigned with Rep. Marcy Kaptur, who is in a competitive race. The two met with owners of a local bar in Sandusky and local attorneys from a firm that does social justice work in Erie County, according to Kaptur’s campaign.

Roughly 90 minutes away, she campaigned with Rep. Shontel Brown at the Greater Cleveland Food Bank.

“Whip Clark showed up in Cleveland, Toledo, and Akron — places we need to win and win big, and that matters,” Brown told The Sun in a statement. “She listened, she engaged, and she spoke the language of people who are juggling child care, health care, and food costs that they can’t afford. Whip Clark is tuned into the wavelength of women and families and we are better for her leadership.”

She has also stumped with candidates in Michigan, New York, Florida, California, Nevada, Arizona, Oregon, Washington and North Carolina.

“In less than one week, change is coming to Washington,” Clark said in a statement. “House Democrats are ready to win and put the people back in the People’s House. We will fight to lower costs, protect healthcare, and hold the crooks accountable.”

Democrats are expected to hold leadership elections in mid-November, and Clark does not face a challenge to keep her post as the second-ranking leader.

entries.title: All-DMV High School Soccer Players of Week 9
entries.summary: This week’s group features a rejuvenated forward from Walter Johnson and a confident freshman from C.H. Flowers.
entries.content:
This story is part of The Washington Sun’s All-DMV coverage. All-DMV is a new collaboration between The Sun, Fox 5 DC, NBC4 Washington and WTOP News, aimed at covering the D.C. area’s best high school athletes. You can find past players of the week and more information about All-DMV here.

With playoffs around the corner, local soccer programs have been scrambling to better their postseason standings. Here’s who stepped up to earn All-DMV Player of the Week:

Marvin Garcia, Senior, Midfield, Fairmont Heights

The Fairmont Heights boys closed out an undefeated regular season last week and made a bit of school history in the process. The Hornets earned a berth in this year’s Prince George’s County title game for the first time in program history.

Garcia, a well-rounded senior midfielder, has been a catalyst all season for coach Ricardo Fuentes’ team. A capable threat on both sides of the field, the Hornets have used his steady play to ascend to the top of the county standings with the playoffs getting underway next week. With Garcia leading the charge, the Hornets scored at least three goals in 10 of their 12 regular-season victories and capped last week with a comfortable 4-1 win over Largo.

“If you hear a voice on the field, it’s his,” Fuentes said. “He’s calming his teammates down, he’s calming even us on the coaching staff down when we’re a little bit too angsty … He’s just a commanding presence.”

Freja Gold, Sophomore, Midfield, Seneca Valley

All season, opposing defenses have keyed in on Gold when facing the Seneca Valley girls. The Screaming Eagles’ top offensive threat has shined regardless, proving to be a goal-scoring machine for coach Lee Benswanger’s team.

Last week epitomized Gold’s season-long dominance. In her team’s regular-season finale against Rockville, Gold scored her fourth hat trick of the season in a 3-2 win. The standout performance brought her regular-season goal tally to 19.

Hunter Parler, Senior, Forward, Walter Johnson

After a scorching start in the preseason, Parler found himself in an offensive slump early in the Wildcats’ regular season. In the hopes of lifting his senior forward out of his scoring funk, coach Samuel Sasu kept it real.

“We sat down, I kind of gave him my open criticism,” Sasu said. “‘Maybe there needs to be an adjustment on your movements, how you’re seeing the game, [or] what you’re thinking about in these moments when you’re going to strike the ball.’”

Parler took Sasu’s feedback and is now on a late-season tear for Walter Johnson. Last week, he tallied a goal and an assist against Northwest. Days later, he one-upped himself with two goals and two assists in a 4-0 win against Kennedy.

“He’s showing the best of himself right now,” Sasu said. “He’s one of the best strikers in the county and in the state of Maryland.”

Jordyn Randall, Freshman, Forward, C.H. Flowers

After winning regionals for the first time in school history last season, the Jaguar girls are looking to ascend to new heights this fall. They’ve relied on Randall, a freshman phenom, to provide the offense and get the team into position for a postseason run.

Randall closed out her regular season on a high earlier this month. Facing Bladensburg, she sealed a 2-0 win with a late goal. Last week, she scored the game-winning goal in overtime to beat Northwestern, 2-1. The golden goal was Randall’s 12th of the season.

“She doesn’t care who you’re playing against,” Flowers coach Whitney Keiller said with a chuckle. “Almost every team we’ve played against has tried to put somebody to mark her, and she’s just been totally unfazed.”

Pia Vasquez, Junior, Forward, Washington International

Vasquez has been a goal-scoring machine for the Washington International girls, who enter the Potomac Valley Athletic Conference playoffs as a bona fide contender after a dominant regular season. Vasquez scored 32 regular-season goals for the Dragons, including a combined four goals last week in wins over Washington Waldorf and D.C. International.

Vasquez scored at least three goals in eight games this season, including a season-high five against Jackson-Reed in late September.

“When I took over the girls team, I picked up Pia as an eighth grader, and she just took the team by storm,” coach Othmane Benkhallouk said. “If she commits and keeps her head down and keeps working hard, this kid can go as far as pro.”

Charlie Waller, Senior, Forward, Gonzaga

The defending WCAC Player of the Year has put together another strong season for the Eagles, who enter the playoffs as the No. 2 seed. Waller finished the regular season with a team-high 17 goals and seven assists.

Gonzaga, which took close losses to St. John’s and The Heights earlier this month, closed out its regular-season slate with three straight conference victories. In that span, Waller scored two goals and an assist, including a crucial goal in a 2-1 win over Good Counsel last week.

entries.title: Everyone Might be Sleeping on Minnesota
entries.summary: Could the Senate race in the blue state throw off Democrats’ majority plans?
entries.content:
Soon after Minnesota’s August primary, a Democratic pollster noticed something worrisome in their data: The statewide candidates — including Peggy Flanagan, who is running for the open Senate seat — were barely polling ahead of their Republican opponents in the blue state.

“I’ve been waiting for the ad alert to come through that Republicans are dropping millions here, and I’m shocked that it hasn’t happened,” the pollster told The Washington Sun.

Nationally, Republicans are bracing for a midterm backlash against the president, the economy and his unpopular war in Iran. As Senate races continue to move largely in Democrats’ favor, Minnesota has stood out as the exception.

Flanagan, the current lieutenant governor, is struggling to separate herself from fraud scandals in the state.

“She’s been tossed the hot potato,” said Matt L. Barron, a Democratic political consultant focused on rural voters.

The fraud fallout appears to be dragging down Flanagan and other statewide candidates. There’s a nightmare scenario for national Democrats in which they manage to flip Senate seats elsewhere, including long-shot battlegrounds, and still miss out on a majority because they lost a race on their home turf.

Flanagan’s campaign is confident that Minnesota voters will see the race as a referendum on the president, rather than state issues. Minnesota is a state where President Donald Trump’s policies have hit close to home — federal agents killed two people in Minneapolis in January after the administration launched immigration operations in the state.

“The polls underestimated Peggy in the primary and she won by 20 points,” Maddie Heinz, a Flanagan campaign spokesperson, said in a statement. “Peggy always says to run like you’re 10 points behind, and that organizing work is how we’ve prevented outside money from pouring into this race.”

The campaign of Republican Michele Tafoya, the star recruit running against Flanagan, did not respond to a request for comment.

This week, Democrats in Minnesota got some welcome news: A New York Times/Siena poll showed Flanagan with a 14 percentage point lead in the race, a data point that shows just how uncertain the terrain is. The Times cautioned that “this is one of the biggest outliers we’ve ever published.” 

Republicans have relentlessly attacked Democrats over the fraud scandals in the state, which pressured Gov. Tim Walz, who has taken the brunt of the political blowback, to end his reelection campaign. In the most well-known fraud case, former leaders of Feeding Our Future, a nonprofit that participated in pandemic-era child nutrition programs, were convicted of participating in a scheme to defraud the federal government of $250 million.

“Feeding Our Future has been the entire focus of the Republican campaigns, including the Senate race,” said Niel Ritchie, the former president of the progressive League of Rural Voters. “It’s fraud, fraud, fraud, fraud, fraud, fraud, fraud, fraud, fraud.”

The Sun previously reported that nearly every competitive Senate election has featured anti-corruption ads, making it one of the stickiest arguments throughout the midterms. National parties are working to link political corruption to voters’ own financial circumstances, arguing that their opponents are taking money from special interests which then raise prices on everyday Americans.

In Minnesota, the messaging from Republicans is even simpler: Flanagan was part of the Walz administration during the COVID-era fraud.

Flanagan, in response, has put the onus on Walz.

“The governor’s been very clear that the buck stops with him,” Flanagan said at a debate in response to a question about the fraud. “He was the one who had oversight here.”

Flanagan is polling slightly behind Sen. Amy Klobuchar, the well-known Democrat who is running for governor. That lag may be more due to Klobuchar’s popularity than anything to do with Flanagan — Other statewide candidates are also polling behind Klobuchar.

But Flanagan is the one running in a key Senate race where both parties are desperately angling for control of the chamber.

The only Flanagan-related news to break into the national political consciousness recently was an odd campaign misstep: Flanagan had said years ago she was a member of the prestigious Phi Beta Kappa academic honor society. Then, in response to a Wall Street Journal inquiry in the final stretch of the campaign, her campaign said she actually wasn’t because she couldn’t afford the fee at the time of her graduation. Then the organization itself said she was a member. Then her campaign also said she was, in fact, a member.

Tafoya is a former sports reporter and broadcaster who isn’t bogged down by a political record and who supports abortion rights. She has tried to distance herself from Trump on some issues, and the state is not so blue that she doesn’t have a pathway to winning — former Vice President Kamala Harris, whose ticket included Walz as her vice presidential pick, won the state by only four percentage points in 2024. In each chamber of the state legislature, Democrats hold a majority by only one seat.

National Republicans’ focus has largely been elsewhere. Millions of Republican dollars are tied up across unexpected battlegrounds scattered across the country, like Kansas and South Carolina where Republicans are bolstering incumbents facing threats.

The National Republican Senatorial Committee did not answer questions about the prioritization of the Minnesota election, or if it plans to increase spending before Election Day.

“Tafoya has closed the gap with Flanagan and her message of accountability is resonating with Minnesotans across the political spectrum,” Nick Puglia, a spokesperson for NRSC, said in a statement. “Peggy Flanagan overseeing at least $9 billion in fraud is an albatross around her neck that Michele Tafoya is exposing as voters make it clear that fraud is a top concern for them.”

Democrats in the state downplay any concern about the race. The chair of Minnesota’s Democratic party praised Flanagan for running “a fantastic campaign” in a statement, and pointed to high early turnout as a good sign for Flanagan.

“Together, DFL campaigns have knocked more than 2.3 million doors,” Richard Carlbom, the state party chair, said in a statement. “Minnesotans are fired up to vote and will reject Trump and his endorsed candidate Michele Tafoya, who would be nothing more than a rubber stamp for his MAGA agenda.”

The race may come down to who voters blame more for their current issues.

“Peggy has got to nationalize it,” said the pollster. “If voters go into the polling place thinking about Tim Walz, we’re going to lose. If they go into the polling place thinking about Donald Trump, we’re going to win.”

entries.title: Defeated Brazilian Presidential Candidate Flávio Bolsonaro Flees to Miami
entries.summary: After refusing to concede to Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Bolsonaro lands in Florida with his family.
entries.content:
By Daniel Kozin and Mauricio Savarese

Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil.

The stunning move came after 48 hours in which Bolsonaro refused to concede to Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and then threatened to attempt to annul the election result.

Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later. On Monday, the U.S. said that it would grant visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family. Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, visited the White House in May.

Bolsonaro first fled from Brazil to Argentina and then Ecuador alongside his wife and two daughters, Argentina's migration authority said Wednesday — a day after the 45-year-old senator and his family were granted United States visas by the Trump administration.

Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil’s Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. The court had ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday — two days after he lost the vote to Lula. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport.

Argentina's migration authority said Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and his daughters Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro crossed into the country at 10:50 p.m. Tuesday. They entered via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a primary border checkpoint linking Brazil to Argentina’s northeastern province of Misiones.

“Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country," the Argentine migration authority said on X.

The authority said that at 11:30 p.m. local time, shortly after clearing immigration control, the four boarded a private charter flight operated by aviation company Baires Fly S.A. According to the filed flight plan, the aircraft departed for Guayaquil, Ecuador.

The move is almost certain to cause a big diplomatic rift between Lula and Argentine President Javier Milei, a Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to take part in Bolsonaro’s campaign.

Flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed that a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro’s landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, before taking off minutes later for Miami-Opa locka Executive Airport. The plane carrying Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami at around 9:30 a.m. EST.

Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, told several dozen supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia before the plane landed that he didn't have precise information about Bolsonaro’s whereabouts, but said he had left Brazil.

“I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true,” Lula said. “This act of leaving Brazil is shameful.”

Paulo Figueiredo, a close Bolsonaro ally who lives in the U.S., said in a short statement that he can't confirm information from foreign authorities, but added “Flávio Bolsonaro is well, in security and resting with his family.” Figueiredo also said there would be a press conference Thursday in Miami to discuss the case.

Representatives of Brazil's government didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press.

U.S. President Donald Trump said early Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., calling him and his family “fine people.”

“The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after returning from campaigning in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate, but stressed that he didn't endorse the election results.

Leaders all over the world and the Organization of American States, or OAS, endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round.

On Tuesday, Milei's administration spokesman Adrián Ravier said “there is no asylum request (from Bolsonaro) and there is nothing more to add.”

The defeated candidate was served with a Supreme Court order to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.

After that defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.

Flávio Bolsonaro said on Monday in a video that he was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country’s Supreme Court.

Brazil's Supreme Court is investigating Bolsonaro for allegedly using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In a separate case, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker.

entries.title: Judge Dresses Down DOJ Attorneys Handling New Hunter Biden Laptop Case
entries.summary: An FBI agent testified that he had been begrudgingly assigned to the investigation and had regarded it as a “huge distraction” from other casework.
entries.content:
By Eric Tucker, Alanna Durkin Richer and Michael Kunzelman

A federal judge on Tuesday scolded prosecutors for their unorthodox handling of a criminal case against two former FBI officials accused of making false statements to Congress about their knowledge of a laptop the Justice Department says belonged to Hunter Biden, the son of former President Joe Biden.

U.S. Magistrate Zia Faruqui rejected an amended criminal complaint filed overnight by the Justice Department that added a new obstruction charge against the two former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, after concluding that it was improperly submitted. Such charging documents require sign-off from a judge that probable cause exists to believe a crime was committed by a defendant, but this complaint was filed to the docket with no court approval.

The ruling came during a dramatic, hourslong hearing in which an agent who worked the case conceded under defense lawyer questioning that the investigation was launched after a July speech from President Donald Trump on election interference and that the inquiry was mandated by FBI Director Kash Patel. The agent, Bryan Witt, suggested he had been begrudgingly assigned to the investigation and had regarded it as a “huge distraction” from other casework.

“I had concerns that this would be political,” he said.

The testimony was elicited by defense lawyers looking to bolster their argument that the prosecution was politically motivated. Faruqui's rebuke, meanwhile, marked a setback for a Justice Department that has employed unusual maneuvers in splashy investigative actions ahead of next week’s midterm elections. Newly unsealed documents in a separate case, for instance, revealed that prosecutors are attempting to again prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, an outspoken Trump critic, in a manner that Comey's lawyers say is legally invalid.

The judge said he had never before seen a prosecutor file an unsigned criminal complaint, describing it as “inappropriate” given defendants’ presumption of innocence. He ticked off several atypical aspects of the case, including the decision to file charges via criminal complaint, which the judge noted is more often used when the government has disrupted an active crime or needs to take a defendant into custody immediately because of a potential danger to society.

“Everything is a little sideshow on top of a sideshow,” Faruqui said, saying prosecutors appeared to be throwing “gas” on defendants’ assertions that there is nothing typical about this case.

The case has political undertones

Witt testified that Patel had directed that the investigation be opened after a Trump primetime address in July in which the president amplified debunked theories about the 2020 election he lost and elevated his yearslong push to raise doubts about the legitimacy of U.S. elections.

Among the grievances the White House raised at the time was a disputed FBI intelligence report about an alleged effort by China to influence the election through fraudulent driver's licenses. Trump and some allies have cited the memo as proof of what they contend was a Chinese plot to intervene in favor of Joe Biden, his Democratic opponent. But senior FBI officials ordered the document recalled because of concerns about the validity of the intelligence.

Witt, who works in Kansas City, Missouri, said Patel assigned the investigation to his office and said he was directed to investigate Floris and other officials who were believed to be involved in recalling the memo.

He said the basis for the investigation was Trump administration suspicions that the FBI in 2020 had suppressed intelligence that could have been harmful to the Bidens. He said he understood the fact that the inquiry was opened in the aftermath of a Trump speech, and at the behest of the FBI director, made it appear like a “political" investigation. Patel and FBI leadership, he said, maintained a keen interest in the probe.

“They wanted us to investigate aggressively,” Witt said.

Even before that testimony was given, Mary Dohrmann, another lawyer for Floris, broached what she called the “elephant in the room,” saying “evidence is mounting that this prosecution is about some political football — and not the law or the facts.”

Defense lawyers disputed the crux of the allegations

The case, announced Friday, accuses Floris and Benavides of falsely playing down their knowledge about a laptop the Justice Department says Hunter Biden abandoned at a computer repair shop in 2019.

Prosecutors say they claimed to have no independent insight into the FBI's possession of the laptop while being interviewed in 2023 in a separate congressional investigation related to the Biden family. In reality, according to the criminal complaint, the two participated in numerous discussions about the laptop in their capacity as leaders of the FBI Foreign Influence Task Force,. which was disbanded by the Trump administration last year.

The Justice Department contends that the defendants' professed lack of knowledge allowed them to avoid further questioning about Hunter Biden and impeded the congressional investigation.

But Ron Safer, a lawyer for Benavides, challenged that assertion during the hearing Tuesday. He suggested that his client had no motive to lie and pointed out that Benavides was questioned in 2023, long after he had left his position on the task force, about events that had occurred several years earlier.

“What evidence have you uncovered that in September of 2023, Mr. Benavides remembered the correct answers, in your view, to the questions asked about Hunter Biden but gave knowingly incorrect answers?” Safer asked Witt.

It is a very intricate saga

The prosecution revisits a tangled saga that roiled the final weeks of the 2020 race after the New York Post revealed the existence of a laptop it said had been dropped off by the younger Biden at a Delaware computer repair shop about a year earlier.

The Post said it had obtained a hard drive of the laptop from Rudy Giuliani, a close ally of President Donald Trump, and reported on some of the contents of the computer, including emails that appeared to show some of Hunter Biden's foreign business dealings.

The curious circumstances of the laptop’s discovery raised concerns among Democrats and former intelligence officials about the possibility of Russian involvement, particularly when the Trump administration’s own intelligence community had assessed that Moscow was attempting to undermine the candidacy of Democratic nominee Joe Biden, who went on to defeat Trump in 2020, and as Giuliani had traveled abroad looking for dirt on the Bidens.

But Trump's then-national intelligence director, John Ratcliffe, quickly sought to quell speculation about the laptop's provenance by saying there were no signs it had anything to do with Russian actors.

The younger Biden was ultimately convicted on gun and tax charges. President Joe Biden pardoned his son in late 2024.

entries.title: Judge Rules Trump’s Top Federal Prosecutor in LA Is Unlawfully Serving
entries.summary: Bill Essayli has become the face of Trump's battle with California over everything from alleged health care fraud to recent claims of widespread noncitizen voting.
entries.content:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Republican Bill Essayli is not legally serving as the top U.S. prosecutor in Los Angeles.

The ruling is the latest roadblock to the Trump administration’s effort to extend handpicked acting U.S. attorneys beyond the 120-day limit set by federal law. The strategy was designed to bypass confirmation by the U.S. Senate — something that generally requires a degree of bipartisan support.

Essayli “is unlawfully serving as a ‘de facto’ United States Attorney,” U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright wrote.

The order won’t take effect until the court rules on the government’s motion for a stay pending appeal. Essayli said he doesn’t agree with the court’s order. He said the president and Attorney General “have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department.”

“Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court, and I look forward to serving in my current role until then,” he said in a statement.

The former state lawmaker was appointed by the Trump administration last year to serve as Acting U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California, which includes Los Angeles. Just before the 120-day mark, then-U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi appointed him as First Assistant U.S. Attorney.

But in October 2025, Seabright disqualified Essayli from overseeing several criminal cases, concluding he had stayed in the temporary job longer than allowed by law. He was allowed to continue to serve as a First Assistant U.S. attorney.

The administration never appointed another acting U.S. attorney, effectively making Essayli the top prosecutor. He’s been a face of the administration’s sparring with California on everything from alleged health care fraud to recent claims of widespread noncitizen voting. California has pushed back on federal efforts to prevent election officials from counting ballots of up to 20,000 people the Trump administration suspects are not U.S. citizens.

On Tuesday, Seabright wrote that Essayli's status faced new questions following an August appeals court ruling in a similar case. The 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that Sigal Chattah, the Trump administration’s initial pick for U.S. attorney in Nevada, was unlawfully appointed to lead federal prosecutions in the state.

Seabright wrote that Bondi’s appointment of Essayli as a special attorney and designation of him as the FAUSA “is identical” to her appointment of Chattah in the same roles.

Despite a new designation by U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche that cut a few of Essayli’s duties, the judge said that “nothing in the revised designation order materially distinguishes it from the Chattah designation order deemed improper in" the appeals court ruling.

Judges have found a number of interim U.S. attorneys installed by the administration are unlawfully serving in their positions.

A judge in New Jersey last year disqualified acting U.S. attorney Alina Habba and in January a judge ruled that John Sarcone was not lawfully serving as acting U.S. attorney for the Northern District of New York.

Essayli is a former federal prosecutor and Republican state lawmaker. In the Legislature, he took up conservative causes and criticized the state’s COVID-19 restrictions. He has been outspoken against California policies to protect immigrants living in the country illegally, and he has aggressively prosecuted people who protest Trump’s ramped up immigration enforcement across Southern California.

entries.title: Pentagon Tells Congress the Iran War Has Cost an Estimated $47.1 Billion
entries.summary: The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16.
entries.content:
By Ben Finley and Konstantin Toropin

The cost of the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to a new estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress. The fallout from the conflict has become a key issue in the midterm elections and could increase as President Donald Trump leaves open the possibility of renewed hostilities.

The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16 and offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched in late February by the United States and Israel. The latest price tag, obtained by The Associated Press this week, shows a $3.5 billion bump in U.S. spending since early September, when that figure stood at about $43.6 billion.

The growing cost of the unpopular war and its economic ripple effects on energy prices could hurt Republicans in next week's midterm elections. Voters on Tuesday will decide which political party controls Congress during Trump's last two years in office.

The Republican president has said new strikes on Iran are an option after the midterms and is sending more military resources to the Middle East, despite initially promising Americans a military campaign that would last only a matter of weeks. As the war’s costs in lives, tax dollars and economic impact grow, most voters say they want Congress to prioritize ending the conflict, according to a recent AP-NORC poll.

The expense of the conflict and military spending in general are already a contentious issue on Capitol Hill, where the Trump administration is pushing for the passage of a historic $1.5 trillion military budget proposal. The White House also is asking lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package that would help fund the Iran war and other priorities.

Wednesday marks eight months of the war, which Democrats have been trying to end through legislation that has failed to pass the Republican-controlled Congress.

“Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. "Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House.”

In the latest estimate, the bulk of the war's costs are for replacing munitions, at about $29 billion. The advanced weapons most in demand and whose stockpiles have been drawn down are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army’s Patriot and THAAD systems, with a single Patriot interceptor costing millions of dollars.

The Pentagon says about $11.9 billion is related to costs of operations, while an additional $6 billion is tied to equipment losses. The Air Force's costs are now $7.6 billion, and the Army's are more than $2 billion. The Navy's costs were listed at $1.45 billion, which is a significant drop from the $2.2 billion listed in early September.

When asked why the Navy’s cost estimates decreased over the roughly six-week period, both the Navy and U.S. Central Command referred the questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment on the new cost estimates.

The latest estimate does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released last month said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

The Pentagon’s official tally lists 21 service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. That count includes troops who died in medical events and other situations that do not have a direct connection to the conflict, with 18 service members having been killed from Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or disposal of Iranian drones.

While Trump has mused repeatedly about whether to make a deal with Iran or “finish them off,” a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. The Trump administration also has reduced staffing at some U.S. Embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel.

entries.title: AJ Dybantsa Will Make His NBA Debut Wednesday Against the Cavs
entries.summary: The No. 1 overall pick in June’s NBA draft missed the Wizards’ first four games with an ankle injury.
entries.content:
AJ Dybantsa is set to make his long-awaited NBA debut on Wednesday against the Cavaliers, the Wizards announced.

The No. 1 overall pick in June’s NBA draft has missed the Wizards’ first four games of the regular season after rolling his left ankle in the preseason finale against the Pelicans on Oct. 16.

Wizards coach Brian Keefe has listed his 6-foot-9 rookie as “day-to-day” since then, and he told reporters before Monday’s loss in Charlotte that Dybantsa would rejoin the team Tuesday in Cleveland and do some on-court work before being reevaluated.

While he was out, Dybantsa was mostly seen working out on an exercise bike at the Wizards practice facility and Capital One Arena.

The Wizards are 2-2 without Dybantsa, with wins over the Bucks and Bulls (two teams not expected to be in the playoffs) and losses to the Raptors and Hornets (both of which have talented rosters).

But the Cavaliers are a notch above both the Raptors and Hornets, having reached last season’s Eastern Conference finals. Dybantsa’s first game will be an immediate test for the 19-year-old rookie and a gauge of how the Wizards stack up against one of the NBA’s best rosters.

entries.title: Dolores Huerta, the Labor Leader, Feminist and Civil Rights Icon, Dies at 96
entries.summary: Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor.
entries.content:
By Susan Montoya Bryan

Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers union to improve working conditions in the nation's fruit and vegetable fields and coined the phrase “Sí, se puede!” that became a widespread rallying cry, has died. She was 96.

Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home.

She kept a busy schedule well into her 90s, marching in protests and speaking in cities across the country about race, poverty, LGBTQ+ and women’s rights on behalf of her Bakersfield, California-based foundation.

Huerta’s resolve cemented her place in history as one of the nation’s most influential labor leaders, civil rights icons and feminist activists. Her three-word Spanish-language slogan — which translates to “Yes, it can be done” — was grounded in the belief that people could affect change.

Her work over the decades earned her a number of accolades, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor. When then-President Barack Obama presented the award in 2012, he praised Huerta as a tenacious leader and joked that he had stolen her slogan for his 2008 campaign.

This year, Huerta sent shockwaves through the Latino community when she revealed that she was sexually abused in the 1960s by the farmworker movement’s co-founder, César Chavez, leading to the birth of two children, a secret she kept for 60 years and long after he died.

From the early 1970s on, Huerta’s life partner was Richard Chavez, César’s brother, and together they had four kids. She also had seven children from two earlier marriages.

Huerta said she had kept silent for so long because she feared that coming forward would compromise her life’s work and unravel all the progress made for workers.

When asked during a 2026 interview with the news organization Latino USA about keeping the secret, Huerta said: “It was my personal pain, it was my personal problem and, you know, I think it was worth it because it was my cross to bear. I’ll say it that way.”

Homegrown activism

Huerta was born Dolores Clara Fernandez in 1930 in Dawson, New Mexico. Her father was a miner and union activist who went on to win a seat in the state Legislature. Her parents divorced when she was 3, and her mother took her and her brothers to California.

Immersed in a melting pot of Mexican, Filipino, African American, Japanese and Chinese working families, Huerta learned from her mother — who owned a restaurant and hotel — about independence, compassion and activism.

Huerta was a young, energetic elementary school teacher in the farm-rich San Joaquin Valley when she decided to answer another calling after growing frustrated by her students’ poor living conditions.

“I couldn’t stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes,” she said in a 2017 PBS Independent Lens documentary on her life. “I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children.”

Huerta’s early work with a civil rights group in Stockton resulted in her meeting Chavez. The two wanted to focus more on the plight of farmworkers, so in 1962 they started the National Farm Workers Association, which became United Farm Workers of America a few years later. She was a key leader and negotiator for the union for years.

She was among those who joined Filipino grape pickers on the picket line in what became the five-year “Delano Grape Strike.” With Chavez, she negotiated collective bargaining agreements and contracts with big growers, winning the first health and benefit plans for farmworkers.

Chavez, who died in 1993, once described her as fearless, committed to the cause and tough when it came to negotiations.

On the campaign trail

She met U.S. Sen. Robert Kennedy of Massachusetts during his visit to Delano in 1968 and became a volunteer on his presidential campaign, registering Mexican Americans in California to vote. Huerta was on stage with Kennedy after he won the California primary and he publicly thanked her moments before he was shot.

The assassination devastated Huerta, but she kept organizing for farmworkers’ rights.

Huerta was jailed 22 times for union demonstrating. In 1988, she was seriously injured while protesting Republican presidential candidate George H.W. Bush’s opposition to the UFW grape boycott during his visit to San Francisco.

Caught in a crowd, she was struck by a police officer’s baton, suffered three broken ribs and a pulverized spleen, and required more than a dozen blood transfusions. She reached a settlement with the city to resolve her claims.

After a long recovery, Huerta shifted focus and hit the road to campaign for women’s rights and encourage Latinas to run for office.

She also campaigned for Democratic Presidents Bill Clinton, Obama and Joe Biden. California Gov. Gavin Newsom considered her a close friend.

Fueled by courage

Emilio Huerta, one of Dolores’ 13 children, once pointed to his mom’s courage during an interview, saying it was one of the most significant drivers of her life’s work.

“To dedicate your life to building a dream of a union for farmworkers, to take on agriculture, which to this today is still a powerhouse. ... That took a lot of guts,” he had said.

Huerta learned the art of lobbying politicians. She secured financial aid for the unemployed and disability insurance for California farmworkers. She spoke out against toxic pesticides, pushed for amnesty for immigrants in the country illegally and fought federal guest worker programs.

By directing nationwide boycotts of grapes and lettuce in the early 1970s, she helped to create the economic pressure and political climate necessary for California to pass what would be the first state law recognizing farmworkers’ right to collective bargaining.

Her work earned her many accolades. She was the first Latina to be inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame and she’s received nine honorary doctorates from U.S. universities.

Schools are named in her honor in California, Texas and Colorado. Her image graces many murals, and streets bear her name, but she didn’t always win favor with more liberal activists.

In 2016 when she endorsed Hillary Clinton instead of Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont in the presidential Democratic primary, actor Rosario Dawson — a Sanders supporter who played Huerta in a 2014 movie about César Chavez — said Huerta had become “an instrument of the establishment.”

Dawson and Huerta eventually reconciled.

Guitarist Carlos Santana later oversaw a documentary based on Huerta’s life after the pair had a late-night conversation about music while in Hawaii. Santana, a Miles Davis fan, discovered Huerta was a huge fan of bebop legend Charlie Parker.

“I even met Charlie Parker. That’s my claim to fame,” Huerta joked during an interview with The Associated Press when she was 87.

It was her work as a leader within the labor movement that reverberated through the U.S. and beyond, making her name synonymous with civil rights. In the 2025 documentary “Seeds of Change: The Life and Legacy of Dolores Huerta,” she recounted her decades-long journey in activism and talked about the inspiration she drew from the women’s movement during the 1970s, saying it provided validation that she too could stand on the stage with other labor leaders.

“I hope that my legacy will be one of an organizer that organized to fight injustice,” she said in the film. “We want to give our children an inheritance of justice, right, not jewels or property or money because they’ll just fight over it. So the main thing to do is to give them this love for justice — and that is the greatest gift I think that any of us can have.”

Associated Press journalist Brian Melley contributed to this report. Former AP journalist Russell Contreras also contributed reporting previously for this story.

entries.title: Democrats May Have Recruited Alaska’s Second Dan Sullivan, After All
entries.summary: Mary Peltola’s campaign staff and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee were both involved in the effort, according to The New York Times.
entries.content:
Democrats have insisted for months that they were not involved in recruiting an Alaska Senate candidate who shares the same name as their Republican opponent, Sen. Dan Sullivan.

But that may not be true, according to a bombshell report published Wednesday that claims Democrats led a monthslong scheme to stack the ballot with candidates and recruit other men named Dan Sullivan, all in the hopes of siphoning off votes from the Republican incumbent.

Involved were both Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign staff and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, according to The New York Times.

A Peltola campaign staffer told the Times that they were asked last summer to find potential candidates named Dan Sullivan. About a year later, a man named Daniel J. Sullivan filed to run for Alaska’s Senate seat.

The other candidate on the general election ballot, Gerald Hiekes — in Alaska, the top four candidates advance from the primary, regardless of party — said he was also recruited to run by a Midwestern man he could not identify to the Times.

In all, Times reporters spoke with at least a dozen people with knowledge of the Democratic plan to stack Alaska’s ballot with candidates. Similar efforts are common in Alaska and across the country, and are generally considered to be legal.

When reached for comment by The Washington Sun, the DSCC denied involvement and cited a number of other historical ballot-stacking efforts in Alaska that have been tied to Republicans.

“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan,” a spokesperson for the organization told The Sun. “Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns — including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle.”

Daniel J. Sullivan has not responded to multiple requests for comment from The Sun throughout the midterm cycle.

The Times also cited text messages between campaign officials and DSCC staff communicating about the plan to spoil Sen. Sullivan’s campaign with other candidates. Peltola did not appear to be included in these texts. Her former campaign manager Elisa Rios, who was fired in August, said she was not directly involved but was “aware” of the plot. Rios contacted the Times last week and asked to retract her statements, the newspaper reported.

The Peltola campaign has repeatedly denied being involved in Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign and it has not responded to The Sun’s request for comment.

Since the announcement of Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy, Republicans have accused him of being a spoiler candidate for Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The accusations culminated in a legal challenge against Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign in June, when the Alaska Division of Elections disqualified the non-incumbent candidate from appearing on the open primary election ballot. Alaska officials echoed the allegations that Daniel J. Sullivan was running in bad faith, arguing that his name would confuse voters supporting incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The case rose to the Alaska Supreme Court, where the challenge was struck down and Sullivan was allowed to remain on the primary ballot. He placed third in the primary election, allowing him to advance to the general election in November — although Alaska election officials demarcated Sen. Sullivan as “Dan S. Sullivan (Registered Republican) Incumbent.”

Staff from both the Peltola campaign and the DSCC celebrated Daniel J. Sullivan’s victory in June, according to text messages reported by the Times.

The legal troubles for Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy were renewed shortly after President Donald Trump, who has dubbed the challenger “Decoy Dan,” visited Alaska in October. The Justice Department filed a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections, again bringing Daniel J. Sullivan’s intentions for running into question.

With Election Day less than a week away, the case has been expedited and a federal judge said Monday that she planned to rule on each party’s motions by late Wednesday afternoon. Early voting for the general election has already begun in Alaska.

entries.title: New Mexico’s Politicians Try On a New Title: Democratic Kingmakers
entries.summary: Sen. Ben Ray Luján played host to a number of potential 2028 candidates, kicking off New Mexico’s inaugural cycle as an early primary state.
entries.content:
If you’re interested in becoming the next Democratic presidential nominee, you’re going to need to learn what a Matanza is.

Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-New Mexico) played host last weekend for the inaugural Fourth in the Nation Matanza Rally on Saturday, an event organizers hope will become a must-visit for would-be presidents hoping to win the Democratic nomination.

“New Mexico has a role and responsibility to be able to shape who the next leader in the United States is going to be in 2028,” Luján said in an interview that aired on the latest episode of The Washington Sun Cast. “I'm just excited for every candidate that is running as a Democrat in 2028 to earn the nomination to be the president, that they learn more about New Mexico.”

The primary map of yore is out. Iowa has been banished by the DNC this year, and South Carolina, once third, has been lifted to the first slot. The other states rounding out the top three are familiar: Nevada. New Hampshire. Then: enter New Mexico.

“We're now fourth in the nation for early primaries,” Luján said. “So we've been reaching out to colleagues, and Mark and Chris were able to get out this weekend, so we welcome them, and we put together just a New Mexico celebration.”

Under the banner of a midterm “Get Out the Vote” event for New Mexico Democrats, Sens. Mark Kelly (D-Arizona) and Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) joined Luján and addressed potential voters and activists more than 15 months ahead of the state’s presidential primary.

Neither visiting senator was coy as to why they were in New Mexico.

“I'm kicking the tires, and it's really important to kick the tires in New Mexico,” Van Hollen said.

“I used to spend a good amount of time in the skies of New Mexico when I was an astronaut,” Kelly said. “I haven’t made a decision [on a presidential run] yet; I’ll do that when we get to the other side of this election.”

Sign up for The Stakeout, The Sun's Congress newsletter you actually want to read. 

DNC officials told The Washington Sun in August the updated calendar is better suited for the party’s diversity, giving Black and Latino voters more of a voice in the presidential primary process.

“Our 2028 nominee, whoever they are, will have to earn this across the whole breadth of America,” DNC Chair Ken Martin said before the vote in August.

What does it take to win a presidential primary in this blue state, carried by Democrats each presidential election since 2008?

“Here in New Mexico, we’re a blue-collar state,” Luján said. “We're a state of workers, whether it's trades or farmers and ranchers, agriculture. We're a state of innovation, of science and technology. We're a state that celebrates generations of families and folks that just moved here within the last few days as well.”

“What I tell everyone that's going to come to New Mexico, though, is learn to eat our chili as well, red and green,” Luján said.

The candidates are taking that advice. Kelly and Van Hollen were not the only Democrats with 2028 on their mind to spend time in the Land of Enchantment this weekend.

New Mexico gubernatorial nominee Deb Haaland was joined Sunday by Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear at a rally of her own. Haaland has also appeared this campaign season with every name on the future candidate long list, including former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren.

Does it help a potential future governor that many potential future presidents want to stand next to her as often as possible?

“If I'm the next governor of New Mexico in the 2028 election season, when our presidential candidates do start coming to New Mexico, that we can direct them to listen to the various communities in our state who are suffering under this president,” Haaland said.

Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina) hosted his 34th annual World Famous Fish Fry this May, a must-stop for Democratic candidates in another early presidential primary state where the former House majority whip carries a lot of sway.

Is Luján on his way to becoming New Mexico’s Democratic kingmaker?

“We're just doing our part to get people together, and this is just the first of what I hope will be many gatherings throughout the state of New Mexico over the next two years,” Luján said.

The Washington Sun Cast is a weekly podcast where Washington Sun reporters talk to lawmakers about their work in Washington and what motivates them. You can download or listen here.

entries.title: U.S. Expels Cuban Official Who Got Into a Diplomatic Dust-Up at the U.N.
entries.summary: Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., claimed that the official “shoved and tried to assault” an American diplomat.
entries.content:
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz confirmed a Cuban diplomat is being expelled from the U.S. after a shouting match on the floor of the General Assembly on Tuesday.

While speaking with Fox News’ Sean Hannity on Tuesday night, Waltz said Secretary of State Marco Rubio signed the paperwork to eject the secretary of the Cuban delegation, who Waltz said “shoved and tried to assault” an American diplomat.

“He’s gone. He’s going to be on a plane to Havana within the next 24 hours. You lay a hand on an American here in the U.S., President Trump, Secretary Rubio and myself, we’re not gonna stand for it,” said Waltz.

The Washington Sun has emailed the Cuban Embassy and State Department for additional information. Waltz did not identify the expelled diplomat by name, but the title appears to correspond to Richard Tur de la Concepción, who is identified as the “first secretary” of the Permanent Mission of Cuba to the United Nations.

The diplomatic dust-up kicked off Tuesday afternoon when Waltz and Cuba’s minister of foreign affairs, Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla, got into an altercation while Waltz delivered a speech about the effects of the Castro regime on the General Assembly floor.

Footage circulating on social media shows Rodríguez approaching the stage as Waltz instructs him not to come closer.

“This individual needs to back away from this podium. He’s not going to intimidate me in the United States of America like he tries to intimidate political prisoners.”

An official in the clip responds, “This individual is the foreign minister for the Republic of Cuba.”

Waltz responds, pounding his fist on the podium and raising his voice, “And I’m the representative for the United States of America. Back up.”

Rodríguez shouts back, “You are a liar.”

The escalation began as Waltz discussed how Fidel Castro sent “thousands of gay people, Christians, Afro-Cubans and others to concentration camps,” prompting the Cuban delegation to begin pounding their hands at their table and request a point of order.

“It was the regime who stripped them of their property,” Waltz continued before stating: “I hope everyone, Mr. President, is listening to the delegation right now.”

Khalilur Rahman, the president of the U.N. General Assembly, requested that Waltz be able to finish his speech before Cuban officials raised their objections.

But Rodríguez continued to walk toward the podium, demanding a point of order.

Rahman struggled to maintain decorum and announced he’d be suspending the meeting.

During the same meeting, Waltz’s press secretary, J.P. Freire, was spotted recording de la Concepción up close, causing the Cuban diplomat to swat the phone away, footage shared by Waltz on social media shows.

In the clip, de la Concepción tells a security guard that Freire is “violating my personal space.”

The security guard then instructs de la Concepción to move to the side, and he disappears from the frame.

The Cuban Mission to the United Nations filed a complaint with the U.N. secretary-general regarding the incident, accusing Freire of harassment, stalking and invasion of personal space to provoke de la Concepción.

“The conduct of the US diplomat constituted a disrespectful act, violative of privacy and incompatible with the decorum and the respect of the personal dignity that should prevail in the United Nations,” the statement said.

The Cuban Mission is requesting the U.N. security department enact preventative measures against Freire to avoid similar future behavior.

entries.title: Afternoon Sun: Bodies, Bodies, Bodies

THE LATEST

entries.title: Kash Patel Invests in U.S. Tech as FBI Investigates Chinese-Connected Cybercrime
entries.summary: The FBI says Patel’s recent stock purchases are “fully compliant” with agency regulations.
entries.content:
FBI Director Kash Patel has personally invested a six-figure sum in U.S. computer technology interests at a time when his department is cracking down on suspected China-connected computer and cyber crime.

Patel disclosed purchasing $50,001 to $100,000 worth of stock in defense contractor American Superconductor Corp. on July 30, according to a new financial disclosure report reviewed by The Washington Sun.

He also reported investing $100,001 to $250,000 in the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares fund. (Government officials are only required to disclose the values of their trades in broad ranges.)

This exchange-traded fund is “triple leveraged” on the success of the top 30 U.S. semiconductor and chip companies, including Nvidia, which recently contributed $25 million to President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project. Trump this month awarded Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, the nation’s highest honor for scientific achievement.

In recent weeks, the FBI has seized “platforms operated and used by China state-sponsored hackers” and arrested a California man on suspicion of smuggling to China over $300 million worth of “high-end computer servers containing U.S.-manufactured graphics processing units” commonly used in artificial intelligence applications.

“The National Security Division will protect the American advantage in the chips that power this technology, a product of our unparalleled innovation and hard work, from illegal diversion by our economic and military adversaries,” Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg said earlier this month.

In a statement to The Sun, the FBI said Patel’s investments are “fully compliant with all Department of Justice rules and regulations. Reporting is done as per the filing instructions.”

In his disclosure filing, Patel told the Office of Government Ethics that “no current conflict exists” with his American Superconductor Corp. investment, but “recusal or divestiture will occur should one arise.” The FBI described Patel’s representation to ethics officials as “standard protocol.”

Patel told the OGE that he was “voluntarily” reporting his Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares investment ahead of schedule. Outside of an annual financial disclosure report due each May, executive branch officials are not required to immediately disclose when they buy or sell exchange-traded funds — just individual stocks, bonds, cryptocurrencies and other similar investments.

Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette, acting vice president of policy and government affairs at nonpartisan watchdog group Project on Government Oversight, said it’s “peculiar that OGE and/or agency ethics officials wouldn't be advising against those kinds of transactions” because the stock ownership gives the appearance of a conflict of interest “at minimum.”

“It could speak to a broader sort of chilling effect or a lax approach to the ethics framework broadly in the administration right now,” Hedtler-Gaudette said.

Massachusetts-based American Superconductor Corp., commonly known as AMSC, does business in a range of industries, including power grids, wind turbines and data center support. It has done much of its government-related business with the U.S. military, according to federal contracting records.

Last decade, the FBI investigated Chinese wind turbine company Sinovel Wind Group LLC, which U.S. officials accused of stealing from American Superconductor Corporation.

Sinovel was “convicted of conspiracy to commit trade secret theft, theft of trade secrets, and wire fraud” causing more than $550 million in losses, according to the Department of Justice.

The theft spurred Trump, then in his first term, to bring the U.S. to the brink of a trade war with China.

"The outcome of this case is a victory for the rule of law. We welcome the opportunity to work with the Trump Administration to ensure that American companies' intellectual property rights are respected and protected throughout the world and to hold those who steal accountable,” American Superconductor Corp. wrote in a statement after the trial’s conclusion.

The stock price of American Superconductor Corp., which did not respond to a request for comment, has tripled during the past three years, according to Yahoo! Finance.

Patel has routinely traded stocks while leading the FBI.

This summer, he violated the STOCK Act by failing to properly disclose an investment in MicroStrategy — now known as Strategy — a company that frequently contracts with the Justice Department.Last year, Patel invested in donut company Krispy Kreme around the same time the FBI was investigating a ransomware group over allegations that it breached Krispy Kreme’s data systems.

In an ethics agreement signed before his confirmation, Patel vowed to “avoid any actual or apparent conflict of interest.”

Patel is hardly the only official in the Trump administration to regularly trade individual stocks.

Dan Scavino, Trump’s deputy chief of staff, recently earned seven figures from his stock holding in Trump’s media company, joining Karoline Leavitt and her family, who disclosed shares in Trump Media as well as shares in defense contractors, Tesla and tech companies.Trump himself has made thousands of individual stock and bond trades in recent months.

“People in government shouldn't be playing the stock market, because there’s always the increased possibility or increased potential of them having sort of access to non-public information that the rest of us don’t,” Hedtler-Gaudette said. “There just needs to be a flat across-the-board ban.”

entries.title: Conservative Activist James O’Keefe Charged Following Minnesota Voting Stunt
entries.summary: O’Keefe and another fellow far-right provocateur were accused of misrepresenting their identities to election workers during Minnesota’s primary election.
entries.content:
Conservative activists James O’Keefe and Cam Higby on Wednesday were hit with unlawful voting and identity theft charges in Minnesota, after allegedly misrepresenting themselves to poll workers during Minnesota’s primary election as part of a video stunt.

In August, the men dressed up in traditional Muslim attire and attempted to apply for a ballot, claiming to be Minnesota voters, prosecutors say.

In Minnesota, voters are not allowed to intentionally misrepresent their identity when applying for a ballot, depositing a ballot in a ballot box, or voting with a voting machine or electronic voting machine. Neither man signed an election oath nor cast a ballot, according to the charges.

In a video posted to social media and viewed by 9.2 million people, O’Keefe, 42, and Higby, 26, visit multiple precincts in Hennepin County and identify themselves using the names of registered voters.

O’Keefe claimed he was going undercover as a journalist to test the state’s voting policy, which allows a registered voter to vouch for up to eight voters applying for same-day registration.

The practice is commonly used in senior living facilities by residents who have not updated their driver's license to reflect their current address. In the 2024 general election, less than 0.6% of votes were cast using the vouching process.

Registered voters whose names were used were not aware of the stunt and did not grant the men permission to use their names. Officials don’t know where the men got the names of the registered voters, and the voters told police they didn’t know how the men got their information.

One of the voters had already cast a ballot, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty told reporters at a news conference on Wednesday, noting the person was shocked to discover the stunt. Some of the names used belonged to deceased voters.

“Polling places are the heart of our democracy and should be places of safety and peace,” said Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon. “Any attempt to disrupt or deceive our election workers will not be tolerated. We are grateful to our law enforcement partners for holding these individuals to account.”

In the video published on Aug. 13, O’Keefe introduces himself and says, “This is vouching for seven other Muslims at a Minneapolis polling booth.”

O’Keefe, who is wearing a white thobe and kufi, is seen with Higby, who is wearing a black abaya with a face-covering veil. The two men walk into different voting locations and O’Keefe asks election officials if he can vouch for eight individuals if they don’t have an ID.

After the workers confirm they can, the men leave and ask the same questions at a different location.

O’Keefe presented the footage as an investigative report, but Moriarty said, “There is no such thing as an undercover investigation in the polling place. You have to identify yourself as a journalist in the polling place.”

The Minnesota Secretary of State’s office alerted her to O’Keefe’s videos, she said.

“Having entered polling places without legitimate purposes and intentionally misrepresenting their identity to election judges in applying for a ballot, the charges filed today are appropriate to address the conduct of Mr. O'Keefe and Mr. Hayden,” said Moriarty.

The two men have not been arrested yet as part of the case, though the county has issued them a summons. A court clerk will send them copies of the complaint with a date to appear in Minnesota for their first hearing.

Moriarty said her office did not issue the charges to send a message ahead of the midterm elections but rather for the men to understand their actions were unlawful.

The charges are low-level offenses in Minnesota. It’s unlikely the men will go to prison, Moriarty said, though the charges each carry a maximum sentence of five years in custody and a $10,000 fine.

entries.title: Judge Issues Broader Block on Trump’s Taxpayer Funded Ads
entries.summary: The new ruling is the second blow to the White House’s campaign-style ads that began airing ahead of the midterms.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Wednesday blocked the Trump administration from creating and airing ads using taxpayer dollars — just weeks after a separate ruling from another court froze federal funds from being used for the estimated $20 million advertising campaign.

The new ruling is the second blow to President Donald Trump’s campaign-style ads that began airing ahead of the midterms. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan agreed with the argument set forth by the Democratic National Committee, which brought the lawsuit, that the Trump administration's use of federal dollars to create and air the ads has the potential to damage the party’s election prospects.

The advertising campaign is facing three separate legal challenges, but the DNC’s complaint is unique because the committee alleges the government unlawfully used public funds to develop and produce the ads, while others allege only that the government is paying for their broadcast.

“Here, there is little doubt that Defendants’ unlawful use of public funds makes it more difficult for the DNC to achieve its mission of ‘electing Democratic candidates in federal, state, and local elections across the Country,’” AliKhan wrote — adding that the Trump administration’s “use of public dollars to finance the challenged ads imposes competitive harm on the DNC, causing Democratic campaign prospects to suffer.”

Earlier this month, U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon of the Southern District of New York blocked the Trump administration from using taxpayer funds to pay broadcast fees associated with the ads, a decision that came in response to a separate legal challenge brought by the nonpartisan watchdog group Common Cause and a coalition of other plaintiffs.

Both of the federal judges' orders extend through the midterms: AliKhan’s order runs through Nov. 11 and Rochon’s order has been extended through Nov. 20.

After facing scrutiny from both sides of the political aisle for the advertising campaign, Trump announced on Oct. 5 that he planned to “pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.,” a super PAC linked to the president. But the DNC filed multiple status reports taking issue with the continued airing of the ads that the committee asserted had been created by White House staff using taxpayer dollars.

AliKhan ordered the Office of Management and Budget and the Department of Homeland Security, which helped execute the multimillion advertising campaign, to “take all necessary actions to cease distribution of the challenged ads, including through authorized third parties.”

“As the DNC explains, and as common sense dictates, election resources are finite,” AliKhan wrote in her ruling. “Thus, every public dollar spent on airing the challenged ads allows MAGA Inc.—which has already spent $25,000,000 in the 2025-26 federal election cycle to support Republican candidates and oppose Democratic candidates—to conserve its resources for other political efforts adverse to the DNC.”

The Trump administration has already aired several of at least 13 ads planned under a $20 million DHS media buy. Ahead of Rochon's decision in the Common Cause case, DHS assured the court it did not have any plans to pursue additional media buys past Oct. 11 — though the ads continued to air for a short time after that date.

But AliKhan wrote that “the court is unpersuaded” by DHS’ declaration, noting that the ads continued to air with the “Paid for by the U.S. Government” disclosure after Trump announced that he planned to pay for them and after Rochon first blocked the advertising campaign earlier this month.

DNC Chair Ken Martin celebrated AliKhan’s decision on Wednesday, calling the ruling a “victory for the rule of law and for American taxpayers.”

“Trump’s illegal and desperate attempt to save his cratering approval ratings ahead of the midterm elections only underscores how out of touch he is with the American people, who will hold him and Republicans accountable for their destructive agenda at the ballot box next week,” Martin said.

A White House official pushed back on the AliKhan’s decision, calling her ruling “moot.”

“The PSAs are being paid for by outside groups,” the official told The Washington Sun. “Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction.”

Former presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden also ran ad campaigns during their time in office — though those spots were intended to highlight specific initiatives rather than a general promotion of patriotism.
