entries.title: Trump Says Peltola Should Face ‘Legal and Political Consequences’ for Dan Sullivan Recruitment
entries.summary: The Democrat’s campaign reportedly recruited Daniel J. Sullivan to run for office to upset incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, The New York Times wrote Wednesday.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump says that Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola should face legal consequences and be barred from appearing on state ballots following reports that her campaign recruited a candidate to run in the election who shared the same name as her opponent, incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Peltola campaign staffers and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee were allegedly involved in a monthslong scheme to stack the ballot with candidates and recruit other men named Dan Sullivan, all in the hopes of siphoning off votes from the Republican incumbent.

“Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done, A FRAUD ON THE AMERICAN PUBLIC, and Dan Sullivan should be allowed to run without either Mary Peltola or FAKE Dan Sullivan on the Ballot,” Trump wrote on Truth Social Wednesday.

The Department of Justice has already filed a lawsuit seeking to block the certification of the Alaska Senate race if the Republican incumbent loses to Peltola.

Daniel J. Sullivan has not responded to multiple requests for comment from The Washington Sun throughout the midterm cycle.

entries.title: Kevin McCarthy Is Working to Boost His Former Foe Jim Jordan
entries.summary: The former speaker is advising Rep. Jim Jordan on how to position himself in a race for minority leader.
entries.content:
MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. — Former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy may be out of Congress, but he’s still playing the inside game.

McCarthy is working as a key advisor to House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan as Jordan potentially seeks the top Republican leadership role in the next Congress, The Washington Sun has learned.

Onetime foes, McCarthy and Jordan became close allies in the final year of the California Republican’s career. As McCarthy sought the speaker's gavel in January 2023, Jordan was a key partner in helping win over some of the conservative holdouts.

After McCarthy was ousted from the post in the fall of 2023, he returned the favor by helping Jordan in his bid for the speakership. That effort failed and McCarthy resigned from the House that December. But now, the duo is back, strategizing about how to boost Jordan’s chances of leading the Republicans conference next year.

McCarthy and Jordan talk often, sources close to both say, and McCarthy has been advising Jordan on how to best position himself for a leadership bid. A source familiar with their conversations said Jordan has sought McCarthy's counsel and confirmed the two have discussed the contours of Jordan’s potential leadership race.

McCarthy declined The Washington Sun’s request to comment.

Top Republican leaders are campaigning across the country to hold on to their narrow House majority, but in the event they lose it, Jordan is expected to run for minority leader, The Sun has previously reported. This would probably pit him against current House Speaker Mike Johnson and McCarthy’s longtime rival and former second-in-command, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise.

The former speaker has criticised Johnson over his handling of the job, and openly predicted his party would lose control of the House in the midterms. Sources point to McCarthy’s jabs at House Republican leadership as subtle indicators that he’s working to assist Jordan. McCarthy cast Johnson’s decision to keep the House out of session over extended periods of time as a mistake, and he suggested leadership was unsuccessful in giving candidates a platform to boast about in their districts.

“In the House, they were in the fewest amount of days. … They let the Democrats dictate,” McCarthy told BloombergTV last week. “You have to give a reason why to win. What are the three things Republicans will do if they win the majority? I can’t tell you what that is."

A source close to McCarthy emphasized to The Sun that members — particularly those whom McCarthy has helped elect in the past — routinely come to McCarthy and seek his counsel for help with their own races, fundraising strategies and other goals.

McCarthy still has strong allies on Capitol Hill, and some of them have privately become Jordan’s top supporters.

“Kevin’s always helping everyone,” one senior GOP member told The Sun. “Well, everyone but Johnson.”

In an interview with The Sun in South Carolina on Monday, Jordan would not engage with the notion that he was planning or thinking about possibly running for Republican leader in two weeks. He repeatedly insisted his sole mission was to keep the House in GOP hands.

“I am not trying to play games, but just I'm focused on the next eight days,” he said. “I'm focused on keeping the majority.”

Asked about McCarthy’s comments about Johnson’s performance, Jordan said that while “you can debate with that all you want, all I know is, here’s where we’re at.”

While no Republican is willing to acknowledge there is positioning going on behind the scenes, allies of Jordan, Johnson and Scalise all have been working to ensure that come Nov. 10, when House Republicans hold their leadership election, their preferred candidate will win.

All three have been barnstorming the country for members and GOP challengers, and attempting to make inroads with the people who will have a vote in the internal conference contest. If Republicans lose the House, the candidate with a simple majority of Republican members’ votes in a secret-ballot race becomes the minority leader. Unlike the public vote on the House floor for the majority leader, this contest hinges on relationships, and even President Donald Trump’s endorsement may not be a factor.

As for whether he believes Johnson is the right person to lead the conference in the minority, Jordan commended the speaker for his work and how he’s handled the past three years. But he demurred from the ultimate question.

“I think Mike's done an outstanding job, but I'm not worried about any of that stuff right now,” Jordan said. “We got to worry about stopping the DSA.”

This story was updated to correct the date of the House Republican leadership elections.

entries.title: We Did the Math: Trump Really Is Talking More About Butts and Bodies
entries.summary: It’s not just Trump’s affinity for Sen. Jon Husted’s rear end — the president has significantly upped his comments about people’s physical appearance this campaign cycle.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump can’t stop talking about Sen. Jon Husted’s butt.

In speech after speech ahead of the midterm elections, Trump has said he “looked him up and down,” said he “examined his ass” and referred to Husted’s backside as “a pile of muscle.” He’s talked about it so much that ahead of Trump’s Wednesday return to Ohio, Husted said he was hitting the gym, presumably working on his glutes, so as to not “let him down.”

Trump has long had a penchant for complimenting — or disparaging — the physical appearances of his allies and enemies alike. But a new analysis by The Washington Sun shows that Trump has referenced physical appearance almost three times as much in the past year as he did during the same period in the 2016 campaign.
TRUMPBUTTS_Graphic.png (3034x2356, AR: 1.29)Husted’s shoulders were so strong Trump joked they hurt his hand. Rapper Nicki Minaj has a “hard to miss” and “beautiful ass.” Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has the "body of a 30-year-old."

These comments draw huge laughs — and sometimes loud cheers — from the crowds. This kind of talk gets such a reaction he’ll talk about a politician he’s particularly impressed by (like Husted) in places far away from where that politician is campaigning.

At a rally in Greenville, South Carolina, last week, the line that drew perhaps the most reaction during the president’s 90 minute speech was — you guessed it — when he called Husted’s rear end “a pile of muscle.” It’s almost easy to forget what the goal of these rallies is: to help reelect the Republicans who are facing an often tough path to return to office in a political climate that is not favorable to their party.

The data clearly shows that Trump’s seeming uptick in body talk isn’t just in our heads. To do our analysis, we took a deep dive into over 4,600 transcripts of the president’s rallies and events, compiled by Roll Call's Factbase. We pulled out appearance-related comments by looking for certain keywords, starting with the basics, like “beautiful,” “handsome” or “pig.” The list grew as we familiarized ourselves with the president’s unconventional vocabulary.

To produce our final estimates, we reviewed thousands (and thousands) of these sentences to see which actually referred to someone’s appearance. We excluded instances where he wasn’t really evaluating that person’s attractiveness, such as clothing comments, the sarcastic nickname “Beautiful Hillary” or discussions of the physiques of transgender athletes.

It was then extremely apparent, especially given his string of rallies and public appearances leading up to Election Day, that the president is cruising toward an all-time record for such remarks this month, even after adjusting for the sheer amount of time Trump has spoken in public leading up to the midterms.

“It’s no secret that President Trump has always had an appreciation for the big and beautiful, Chris Christie excepted,” a MAGA strategist told The Sun. The strategist said the president’s focus is not just well received in real life, but also online, especially for Republicans who need some levity before what’s expected to be a bruising midterm election.

“Only Trump could compliment a man’s ass at a rally and somehow come out of it looking like the most confident guy in the room,” they added.

Trump has always freely dispensed physical evaluations of other people — think of his “beautiful” former Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, or Tom Homan’s “central casting” looks. One longtime Trump friend told The Sun that they didn’t “recall him being fixated on the subject,” as he is now, though looks and aesthetics have always been central to him. To that point, we’ve found that the tenor of his comments has evolved several times.

His previous high-water mark in the appearance index, around the 2024 campaign and its aftermath, was driven in part by a heavy rotation of stock insults — you may recall lines about California Sen. Adam Schiff’s “pencil-neck” and Christie’s weight.

But his latest surge seems to come from a more generous place. Compliments referring to his political allies as “handsome” and “good-looking” have lifted his apparent appearance obsession to new heights.
TRUMPBUTTS_Graphic copy.png (3034x2152, AR: 1.41)He also comments on men’s appearance far more often than he does on women’s — especially when you exclude formalities such as “and his beautiful wife” or references to “beautiful” victims of alleged crimes.

David Hamermesh, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Austin who wrote an entire book on the economics of physical attractiveness, told The Sun that humans constantly evaluate the attractiveness of the people we meet. The difference when it comes to Trump is the extent to which he makes those opinions known.

The tone change, however, is a good thing, Hamermesh said.

“He’s at least saying nice things about good-looking people,” he said. “He’s not insulting people for a change.”

But, he added: “The president shouldn’t be doing this. It has nothing to do with the job.”

The body-comment mania shows no signs of stopping, and if anything, seems to be spreading.

Not everyone is getting the Husted treatment, however. During a Tuesday night rally in Corpus Christi, Texas, when attempting to explain his prior comments about Husted, Trump said that the Ohio senator’s polling numbers had gone up by 12 points following his remarks.

“Maybe I should do that with Ken Paxton,” Trump joked. “But I don’t think your body is going to qualify.”

entries.title: Federal Reserve Maintains Interest Rates Ahead of the Midterms
entries.summary: The Federal Reserve said economic “uncertainty remains elevated.”
entries.content:
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday in the committee’s last move before the midterm elections, which have been dominated by affordability concerns.

“While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient,” the Federal Open Market Committee said in a statement.

The committee voted 10-2 to maintain rates at 3.75% to 4%. The members cited strong productivity growth and capital investment, as well as job gains, in their decision, their second to last of the year. The two dissenting committee members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, wanted to raise interest rates a quarter percentage point.

In September, the Fed raised rates a quarter percentage point to tamp down on inflation — its first rate hike since 2023. The higher target range, which influences rates for consumer and business loans, sent average mortgage rates climbing to 7.32% for a 30-year loan, according to Freddie Mac. Mortgage rates started the year at 6.15%.

Americans are facing higher prices across the board. The Fed’s primary metric for annual inflation increased 3.4% in August and increased 0.3% from the month prior, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. The Fed has a 2% target inflation rate.

Republicans have struggled to buoy Americans’ spirits about the cost of living. Many Trump administration officials and lawmakers have said energy prices will come down when the Iran war ends, but economists say high energy costs have tainted the supply chain and made products more expensive for months to come.

On the campaign trail, high gas, food and housing prices have become central issues and Democrats’ primary line of attack as they attempt to retake Congress.

President Donald Trump and his party have insisted the Fed should lower rates to stimulate economic growth and bring prices down, though Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has said the central bank will maintain its independence. Lowering rates makes borrowing cheaper, encouraging new businesses to open and existing ones to expand their operations at the risk of overheating the economy.

Members of the rate-setting committee, however, indicated in their quarterly economic projections last month that another rate hike could be on the horizon. Most committee members estimated interest rates should top 4% this year and into 2027 to fulfill the Fed’s dual mandate of keeping prices stable and promoting employment.

The final interest rate meeting of the year will take place Dec. 8 and 9.

entries.title: Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Orders Investigation Into Vance’s Donor Network
entries.summary: The justice ordered Brazil’s federal police to investigate any connections between Rockbridge Network and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign.
entries.content:
Vice President JD Vance’s donor network is under scrutiny in Brazil after a local Supreme Court justice on Tuesday called for the country’s federal police to investigate any alleged connection between the organization and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign.

In a 38-page decision written in Portuguese, Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino cited “reports of a potential influx of foreign funds to benefit an election campaign” and wrote that the Rockbridge Network, which Vance co-founded, allegedly participated in discussions meant to secure financial backing for Bolsonaro.

It is illegal in Brazil for political parties and candidates to receive foreign contributions, either directly or indirectly. Dino noted in the ruling that the U.S. has similar bans.

The investigation seeks “the identity of those responsible for paying for and contracting the electoral advertising attributed to foreign profiles,” as well as the source of the funding.

Vance co-founded Rockbridge Network with conservative media figure Chris Buskirk in 2019. The vice president’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but Rockbridge denied contact or involvement with the people cited in Dino’s order who had said they were agents for the network, The Washington Post reported.

“The Brazilians made false representations about their relationship with Rockbridge and created documents representing or referencing Rockbridge without Rockbridge’s knowledge or consent,” the network told the Post in a written statement.

Dino’s ruling Tuesday is the latest entry in a pattern of escalating tensions between the two countries, particularly as President Donald Trump has levied significant tariffs on Brazil after tense relations with President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. In August, the State Department also revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the U.S. after Brazilian officials declined to grant diplomatic approval to Daniel Perez, the U.S. ambassador to Brazil.

The ruling cites several of those tension points, including the ambassador negotiations and ongoing legal tensions with tech giant Meta.

Brasil Pronto pra Mais, an entity associated with Lula’s campaign, sued Meta earlier this month, alleging preferential treatment for Bolsonaro’s campaign on the company’s social platform. Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court ruled Oct. 15 that the tech giant must ensure Lula and Bolsonaro receive equal treatment ahead of the runoff election, though Meta had already denied wrongdoing.

Dino’s order also directed Brazil’s federal police to look into “algorithmic manipulations” by tech companies intended to help certain candidates in the election.

After Lula beat Bolsonaro in a runoff election this week, the conservative senator fled the country in an apparent attempt to avoid a federal corruption investigation into his family enterprises. The Trump administration granted Bolsonaro and his family U.S. visas, the Post reported Wednesday.

Bolsonaro left after the country’s Supreme Court ordered him to surrender his passports and barred him from international travel as part of a criminal probe into a $10 million money-laundering and corruption scheme, CNN reported. He has denied wrongdoing and referred to himself Wednesday as the “true president-elect.”

entries.title: Tesla, SpaceX and PepsiCo: Jeanine Pirro Made 140 Financial Trades Since April
entries.summary: Many trades by the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia appear to have been reported late, federal records indicate.
entries.content:
U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro reported 140 personal financial trades since April, according to federal records maintained by the Office of Government Ethics.

Pirro’s trades include two stock purchases in companies led by Elon Musk, a top ally of President Donald Trump. She bought $1,001 to $15,000 worth of stock in Tesla Inc. on April 1 and $50,001 to $100,000 in SpaceX on Aug. 13, federal records indicate.

Pirro, who previously hosted “Justice with Judge Jeanine” on Fox News, appears to have disclosed the Tesla purchase and dozens of other individual stock trades after a 45-day federal deadline for doing so. Pirro’s disclosure says she received “a 90 day filing extension” — something not typically extended by law to periodic stock trade disclosures.

“DOJ ethics officials review U.S. Attorney Pirro’s financial disclosures and ensure she is properly recused from any matters involving entities in which she has a covered financial interest,” Tim Lauer, a spokesperson for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia, told The Washington Sun. “In instances where a recusal is required the Principal Assistant United States Attorney serves as the attorney of record.”

Lauer’s statement did not address The Sun’s inquiry about the “90 day filing extension” or the potentially late trades.

Pirro made sizable single purchases in a number of individual stocks and exchange-traded funds: $250,001 to $500,000 in Federated Hermes Government Obligations Fund, $100,001 to $250,000 in PepsiCo, $50,001 to $100,000 in AT&T, and a number of other smaller buys throughout the year.

Pirro owns at least $15,001 worth of stock or bonds in each of around 40 companies. That dollar amount is the threshold at which she must recuse herself from matters should any one of those companies become party to a dispute.

Among those companies are Microsoft, Nvidia, JPMorgan, Uber, Netflix and Exxon Mobil.

Pirro is also an investor in restaurant CAVA and would be conflicted out of any case where the D.C.-based company is a party.

In an ethics agreement Pirro signed in July 2025, she agreed to divest some of her existing investments, including Ares Capital Corporation.

“The Office of Government Ethics (OGE) reviewed that holding last year and determined she needed to divest, which she did immediately in accordance with their guidance,” Lauer said.

In late June and July this year, Pirro bought VanEck BDC Income ETF, giving her a stake valued at $200,002 to $500,000. Ares Capital Corporation makes up over 14% of the fund, meaning she effectively owns $29,000 to $72,000 of Ares stock.

“She continues to work closely with OGE to ensure full compliance with all ethics requirements,” Lauer told The Sun. “OGE does not consider an investment holding within an ETF or mutual fund (of which there are many) to be a violation of the individual’s ethics agreement obligations regarding repurchasing, and she will continue coordinating with ethics officials to ensure she meets all obligations.”

Unlike many higher-ranking Trump administration officials, Pirro has continued to trade individual stocks during her service in government. Pirro is fully apprised of the funds she is personally trading, as her federal transaction reports bear her signature.

Pirro’s ethics agreement, signed before her confirmation last year, says that even if her trades were made by an “investment professional,” she would need to give “prior approval” for certain trades, such as the VanEck BDC Income ETF purchase.

entries.title: Trump Administration Touts Triumphal Arch as Drone Defense Complex
entries.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the arch would be a “generational national defense opportunity.”
entries.content:
The Trump administration is doubling down on plans to use the president’s proposed triumphal arch as a military complex, characterizing the massive structure as a way to protect the capital against drone threats.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in court filings Wednesday that the arch could bring officials from their agencies and others under one roof to better protect the nation from coordinated drone attacks. The administration had yet to rely heavily on the military justification for the arch in previous court filings.

In a Wednesday affidavit, Mullin said current facilities lack the “specialized methods, processes, and tools” required to properly monitor drones in Washington, leaving agencies “poorly positioned” to counteract “evolving” nefarious drone activity.

That leaves the region vulnerable to spies, violent extremists and criminals who could use drones to carry explosives, conduct hostile surveillance of government buildings, fly in unauthorized airspace or carry out other instances of “targeted violence,” Mullin said.

Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch is tall enough to provide a line-of-sight advantage and has the capacity to host security features such as drone detection sensors without requiring any changes to the existing design, Mullin said.

Final design plans submitted to a federal review board earlier this month make no mention of drones, ammunition storage, sniper mounts, drone detection sensors or other similar infrastructure. The plans also don't mention “national security” concerns.

In his own affidavit filed Wednesday, Hegseth said the capital’s landscape and high concentration of government agencies is vulnerable to the “well established” threat of drones being used by bad actors.

He too praised the arch’s height as a significant advantage in fending off drones, as it could allow sensors and communications equipment to be placed above the surrounding landscape to get a clearer picture of incoming threats.

“The Arch is a generational national defense opportunity to mitigate these evolving threats,” he said. The affidavit spelled out several purposes — military command, drone sensor integration, counter-drone strike systems, communication connectivity, observation and overwatch — the arch could support.

President Donald Trump first touted the arch as a monument to commemorate the nation’s 250th birthday when he announced plans for the structure last year. He shifted the framing in September amid ongoing legal challenges and started calling the planned arch a “military complex." The language is similar to justifications Trump used for the White House ballroom, which he originally said was needed to host VIP guests before insisting the building is vital to national security.

The Trump administration is hoping to get final approval for the arch, planned to be built in a traffic circle situated at the west end of the Arlington Memorial Bridge, from a federal commission stacked with Trump appointees on Nov. 5.

But three Vietnam War veterans, who argue the arch will impede on the nearby Arlington National Cemetery, filed a lawsuit in February to stop the arch and are seeking a preliminary injunction to bar construction by Nov. 4. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan will hear arguments Friday in that case about whether to block construction of the arch.

The arch has faced multiple legal challenges, including a lawsuit filed by Arlington County arguing the administration failed to complete a legally required environmental review before barreling ahead with the development.

Local preservation officials have also pushed back against the monument, saying administration officials have underestimated how much the “integrity of the affected historic properties would be diminished” by its construction.

entries.title: Trump Ordered East Potomac Park to Close Twice, Administration Says
entries.summary: The statement marks a change from what a Justice Department lawyer told the court earlier this month.
entries.content:
The Trump administration confirmed to a federal judge Wednesday that the government is "working to develop a plan" to close East Potomac Golf Links for redevelopment by Nov. 15.

In a court filing, the government said the president twice directed the Department of the Interior and the National Park Service to close the course that day — a change from what a Justice Department lawyer told the court earlier this month.

The government also said it will provide 10 business days’ notice of the park’s closure, in response to a Monday ruling by U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes that also ordered an extension of the ban against tree removals at the public golf course.

The Justice Department appealed that ruling to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia on Tuesday, without explaining why the court should overturn it.

In her ruling Monday, Reyes requested a response from the Trump administration about whether any plan existed to shutter East Potomac Golf Links on or around Nov. 15. President Donald Trump had reiterated on social media following the injunction ruling that the golf course would close on that day for a 15-month period to turn it into a “world class championship” facility.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward told Reyes in a hearing on Oct. 19 that there were no plans to close the course by the date the president stated, the day after Trump first posted on Truth Social that restoration would begin on Nov. 15, along with a rendering of what the new course would look like.

entries.title: Civil Rights Groups Sue to Stop DHS Voter Fraud Investigations
entries.summary: The complaint also seeks to prevent DHS from demanding that state officials refuse to provide ballots to people who appear on its noncitizen voter list.
entries.content:
Civil rights groups sued Wednesday to stop the Department of Homeland Security from investigating foreign-born citizens as part of the voter fraud probe intensifying ahead of the midterm elections next week.

The lawsuit also seeks to prevent DHS from demanding that state officials refuse to provide ballots to people who appear on its noncitizen voter list or not count those ballots.

The groups filed the lawsuit as the Trump administration has demanded that California and Washington state segregate ballots from people DHS suspects aren’t citizens.

The department has touted arrests for voter fraud of legal permanent residents and immigrants without legal status. Federal agents have also gone door-knocking in the search for cases of noncitizens voting, which is extremely rare.

DHS’s voter fraud investigation targets naturalized citizens and exposes them to disenfranchisement, the civil rights groups argue.

"This administration knows its data is flawed and unreliable, but they’re using it anyway to scare eligible voters away from the polls. It’s a deliberate effort to spread unfounded lies and make people doubt our elections," said Virginia Kase Solomón, the president and CEO of Common Cause, in a press release. "When even one voter is targeted, all of us are at risk.”

The lawsuit cites a whistleblower report last month about immigration officers using unreliable information to create records stating U.S. citizens voted before obtaining citizenship.

Local election officials in California have questioned the accuracy of DHS’s list of likely noncitizen voters, CalMatters reported. A federal judge in the state concluded last week that DHS was using unreliable data to send federal agents to people’s homes, restricting DHS door-knocking operations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington state and Wisconsin.

Earlier this week, a divided panel of the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals dismissed for now the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force California to segregate 20,000 mail ballots from voters the administration suspects are not citizens. A judge is expected to issue a ruling in that case Wednesday.

In a press release on the recent arrests, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said: “The Trump Administration will not allow illegal aliens to steal the votes of hardworking American citizens. American elections are for Americans only.”
